steps.label: Ki
steps.body: At 10 µM X the apparent Km doubled (1 → 2 mM), so 1 + 10/Ki = 2 and Ki = 10 µM.

steps.label: New Km
steps.body: At 20 µM X, apparent Km = 1 mM × (1 + 20/10) = 3 mM.

items.takeaway: For competitive inhibitors, apparent Km = Km(1 + [I]/Ki), and saturating substrate still gets close to Vmax.

items.prompt: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis?

options.why: It's regulated and catalyzes the last step, but it isn't the committed step.
PFK-1 makes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the first step unique to glycolysis.
Hexokinase catalyzes the first step, but glucose-6-phosphate can still enter other pathways.
An important energy-yielding step, but not the main control point.

items.tldr: PFK-1 commits glucose to glycolysis by making fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

steps.label: Committed step
steps.body: The first irreversible step that leads only to glycolysis.

steps.label: Identify
steps.body: Fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, catalyzed by PFK-1.

steps.label: Regulation
steps.body: ATP and citrate inhibit it; AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it.

items.takeaway: PFK-1 is glycolysis's main control point: energy-rich signals slow it, and energy-poor signals speed it up.

items.prompt: What causes the rapid depolarization phase of a neuron's action potential?

options.text: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps three Na⁺ out for every two K⁺ in.
options.why: The pump maintains the gradients but is too slow to drive the spike.

options.text: Cl⁻ ions flow into the cell.
options.why: Cl⁻ influx makes the inside more negative, which hyperpolarizes.

options.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ flows into the cell.
options.why: The inward rush of Na⁺ drives the membrane potential sharply positive.

options.text: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ flows out of the cell.
options.why: That's repolarization, which follows depolarization.

items.tldr: Depolarization is Na⁺ rushing in through voltage-gated channels.

steps.label: Threshold
steps.body: Once the membrane reaches threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

steps.label: Spike
steps.body: Na⁺ flows down its gradient into the cell, rapidly depolarizing it.

steps.label: Recovery
steps.body: Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open, repolarizing the cell.

items.takeaway: Na⁺ in: depolarize. K⁺ out: repolarize. The pump resets the gradients.

items.prompt: Which cells directly kill virus-infected host cells that display viral antigens on MHC class I molecules?

options.why: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they don't kill cells.
Helper T cells read MHC class II and coordinate the response; they don't kill directly.
CD8⁺ T cells recognize antigen on MHC I and destroy the infected cell.
Neutrophils mostly engulf bacteria; they don't read MHC I.

items.tldr: MHC I + viral antigen is the signal CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells act on.

steps.label: MHC I
steps.body: Nearly all nucleated cells display internal (including viral) peptides on MHC I.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: CD8 binds MHC I, so CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize and kill the cell.

items.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Gardens should be designed without any regard for politics.
options.why: The author describes gardens' politics but recommends nothing.

options.text: Formal and landscape gardens both expressed claims about human control of nature, and the landscape style hid that control rather than giving it up.
options.why: The passage treats both styles as arguments (P1–P3) and concludes that the landscape style concealed power (P4).

options.text: English landscape gardens were more natural than French formal gardens.
options.why: The author says the landscape was "no less a construction."

options.text: Formal gardens reflected royal power, while landscape gardens carried no political meaning.
options.why: Admirers tied the landscape style to English political liberty.

items.tldr: Both styles argued about control; one displayed it, the other disguised it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 gardens as arguments. P2 formal control. P3 landscape "freedom" that was also built. P4 two ways of displaying power.

steps.label: Main idea
steps.body: The contrast in P4, supported by P2 and P3.

items.takeaway: When a passage ends by reframing a contrast, that reframing is usually the main idea.

items.prompt: According to the passage, landscape gardeners sometimes

options.text: clipped hedges into walls and cones.
options.why: Clipped hedges are a feature of the formal garden.
Fountains belong to the French formal garden.

options.text: moved villages so that they would not interrupt an owner's view.
options.why: Paragraph 3 says villages were sometimes moved out of the view.

options.text: laid out long straight avenues toward the horizon.
options.why: Landscape gardeners removed straight lines.

items.tldr: Landscape gardeners even moved villages to keep the view "natural."

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The last sentence of paragraph 3.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Villages moved out of the view.

items.takeaway: Keep each feature attached to the style the passage gives it to.

items.prompt: The author mentions that admirers connected the landscape style with "English political liberty" primarily in order to

options.text: prove that England was a freer country than France.
options.why: The author reports the admirers' view without endorsing it.

options.text: explain why the formal style became popular in France.
options.why: The remark concerns the English style.

options.text: criticize the admirers for ignoring beauty.
options.why: The author never faults the admirers' taste.

options.text: show that the landscape style, like the formal style, carried a political meaning.
options.why: It extends the passage's claim that gardens are arguments to the English style too.

items.tldr: The liberty link shows that the "natural" style was political too.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: It comes right before "But the natural landscape was no less a construction."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It sets up the claim that both styles made political arguments.

items.takeaway: A view the author reports and then complicates usually sets up the author's own point.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following is most analogous to the landscape garden?

options.text: An office designed to feel casual and free of hierarchy, while managers still monitor employees closely
options.why: Control persists but is hidden behind an appearance of freedom, the author's reading of the landscape garden.

options.text: A palace throne room that raises the ruler high above the floor
options.why: That displays power openly, like the formal garden.

options.text: A vegetable plot laid out in straight rows for easy harvesting
options.why: Practical order isn't the disguised power the analogy needs.

options.text: A wilderness area that people have never altered
options.why: The landscape garden was heavily altered; it only looked untouched.

items.tldr: Hidden control behind a look of freedom is the landscape garden's pattern.

steps.label: Abstract it
steps.body: Real control, presented as effortless freedom.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The casual office with close monitoring fits.

items.takeaway: For analogies, match the structure (hidden control), not the subject matter.

items.prompt: The question in the passage's final sentence suggests that the author

options.text: considers the question of honesty unimportant.
options.why: The author calls it worth asking.

options.text: wants readers to stop visiting historic gardens.
options.why: Nothing in the passage discourages visiting gardens.

options.text: believes the formal garden was more honest than the landscape garden.
options.why: The author poses the question without answering it.

options.text: thinks open and concealed displays of power are worth comparing in other areas of life.
options.why: The author says the question of honesty is "worth asking of more than gardens."

items.tldr: The author leaves the question open but wants it asked widely.

steps.label: Read the sentence
steps.body: "Which is more honest is a question worth asking of more than gardens."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: The author values the comparison beyond gardens but doesn't settle it.

items.takeaway: A closing question usually signals what the author wants readers to consider, not a hidden answer.

items.prompt: The central thesis of the passage is that

options.text: Montaigne wrote about himself mainly out of vanity.
options.why: The author says his self-examination "was not vanity."

options.text: Montaigne's essays were open-ended attempts to think, a form shaped by his changeable mind and largely abandoned by the school essay.
options.why: This covers the origin of the form (P1), its shape (P2–P3) and the later departure from it (P4).

options.text: Montaigne's essays are disorganized and should not be imitated.
options.why: That is the critics' charge, which the author rejects.

options.text: the five-paragraph essay is the best way to teach writing.
options.why: The author says such writing shouldn't be called an essay at all.

items.tldr: The essay began as a way of finding out what one thinks.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 the new form. P2 why Montaigne studied himself. P3 the form follows the mind. P4 schools forgot this.

steps.label: Thesis
steps.body: The essay is an attempt, true to a changing mind.

items.takeaway: The thesis usually ties together the passage's history and its argument.

items.prompt: According to the passage, Montaigne studied himself mainly because

options.text: he had nothing else to write about.
options.why: He wrote about many subjects, from friendship to education.

options.text: serious books were expected to focus on their authors.
options.why: Serious books were expected to concern God, law and great men.

options.text: he was the only person he could observe from the inside.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says he was "the one specimen of humanity he could observe from the inside."
The author says his self-examination was not vanity.

items.tldr: He was the one case he could study from within.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The second half of paragraph 2.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The only specimen he could observe from the inside.

items.takeaway: Detail answers paraphrase a specific sentence; find it before choosing.

items.prompt: The author uses the word "fidelity" (paragraph 3) in order to

options.text: reframe the essays' wandering structure as a faithful record of a changing mind.
options.why: The author offers "fidelity" in place of the critics' "disorder."
Religion isn't the subject of this paragraph.

options.text: criticize Montaigne for being disloyal to his sources.
options.why: The word is about faithfulness to his own mind, not disloyalty.

options.text: concede that the critics were right about the essays' disorder.
options.why: The author rejects "disorder" as the right description.

items.tldr: "Fidelity" turns a flaw (disorder) into a virtue (faithfulness).

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "Critics have called this disorder. It is better described as fidelity..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: A positive reframing of the same feature.

items.takeaway: "Better described as" signals that the author is replacing someone else's label.

items.prompt: Which of the following would the author most likely consider closest to the original spirit of the essay?

options.text: A reflection that begins with a question about forgiveness, weighs several examples, changes its mind midway and ends uncertain
options.why: It thinks its way forward without a foreknown conclusion, like Montaigne's attempts.

options.text: A legal brief arguing for a client's innocence
options.why: A brief announces a fixed conclusion rather than finding one.

options.text: A report that states its conclusion first and supports it with three pieces of evidence
options.why: That is the school essay of demonstration the author contrasts with the original form.

options.text: A biography of a king that lists his deeds in order
options.why: That resembles the "serious books" Montaigne departed from.

items.tldr: An essay in Montaigne's sense discovers its conclusion as it goes.

steps.label: The ideal
steps.body: Finding out what one thinks, not announcing it.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only the forgiveness reflection changes as it thinks.

items.takeaway: Apply the author's defining contrast (finding out vs. announcing) to each choice.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward well-organized school essays is best described as

options.why: The author explicitly sees nothing wrong with a well-organized argument.
The author takes a clear position on what they should be called.

options.text: accepting of their usefulness, but critical of calling them essays.
options.why: The author says there is "nothing wrong" with them but that calling them essays forgets the form's origin.
The author says they betray the form's origin.

items.tldr: Fine as arguments, wrongly named as essays.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "There is nothing wrong with a well-organized argument. But to call it an essay is to forget..."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: A qualified criticism.

items.takeaway: "There is nothing wrong with X. But..." marks a mixed attitude, not contempt.

items.prompt: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.text: Because every photograph involves choices, the ethics of Fenton's image depends on whether it leads viewers to true beliefs, not on whether he arranged anything.
options.why: P3 argues that choices are unavoidable, and P4 relocates the ethical question to what viewers are led to believe.

options.text: Photographs are no more reliable than paintings.
options.why: The author questions a simple trace-versus-interpretation contrast but never equates the two.

options.text: Fenton certainly moved the cannonballs onto the road.
options.why: The author never settles which photograph came first.

options.text: Photographers should never arrange their subjects.
options.why: The author says arranging and selecting blur together and focuses instead on viewers' beliefs.

items.tldr: All photos involve choices; what matters is whether they mislead.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 the controversy. P2 why it matters. P3 choices are unavoidable. P4 the real ethical test.

steps.label: Main point
steps.body: The test in P4, grounded in P3.

items.takeaway: When the author says "This does not mean...", the next sentences often state the real thesis.

items.prompt: The passage suggests that knowing which photograph came first would reveal

options.why: Technical quality isn't at issue.

options.text: whether the cannonballs were moved onto the road or off of it.
options.why: The order tells whether the scattered-road version was staged, as paragraph 1 explains.

options.text: whether Fenton was actually present at the war.
options.why: Fenton's presence isn't in doubt in the passage.

options.text: how many soldiers died on the road.
options.why: Casualties aren't discussed.

items.tldr: The order settles whether the drama was staged.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: "...which came first, and therefore about whether Fenton moved the cannonballs..."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: The sequence reveals the direction of any moving.

items.takeaway: "And therefore" links two claims; the inference usually rides on that link.

items.prompt: The discussion of Fenton's equipment and long exposures in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.text: criticize the quality of early cameras.
options.why: The point concerns choices, not image quality.

options.text: support the claim that selecting a scene and arranging one are hard to separate.
options.why: If everything had to hold still, Fenton's pictures were partly arranged by necessity.

options.text: prove that Fenton did not move the cannonballs.
options.why: It shows his methods involved arranging, not what he did with the cannonballs.

options.text: explain why the photographs were taken in a ravine.
options.why: The location isn't explained by the equipment.

items.tldr: Slow cameras meant arranged scenes, so the line blurs.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: The detail sits between "every photograph involves choices" and "the line... is less sharp."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: Evidence for the blurred line.

items.takeaway: Details placed between a claim and its restatement are evidence for it.

items.prompt: According to the author's view, which of the following photographs raises the most serious ethical concern?

options.text: A wildlife photo taken from a carefully chosen angle that shows an animal's real behavior
options.why: Choices were made, but the belief the photo creates is true.

options.text: A portrait for which the subject was asked to sit by a window for better light
options.why: The pose was arranged, but viewers aren't misled about anything that matters.

options.text: A news photo for which debris was placed on a dry street to suggest that the street had flooded
options.why: It leads viewers to a false belief about events, the author's test for an ethical problem.

options.text: A wedding photo in which the guests were asked to smile
options.why: Arranged, but no one is deceived about the event.

items.tldr: The problem is a photo that leads viewers to believe something false.

steps.label: The test
steps.body: What does the photo lead viewers to believe, and is it true?

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: Only the staged flood creates a false belief about events.

items.takeaway: Apply the author's criterion, not your own sense of what seems staged.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the controversy over Fenton's photographs is best described as

options.why: The author never concludes that Fenton was dishonest.

options.text: dismissive, since the author thinks nothing was at stake.
options.why: "This does not mean that nothing was at stake."

options.text: respectful of what is at stake, but skeptical of the controversy's main assumption.
options.why: The author says something real was at stake but questions the sharp line between selecting and arranging.
The author engages the question closely.

items.tldr: Something real is at stake, but the controversy draws the wrong line.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: P3 questions the line; P4 insists something was at stake.

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Engaged and qualified.

items.takeaway: Authors who say "This does not mean..." are usually guarding a middle position.

items.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.text: explaining why ruins pleased eighteenth-century viewers, and arguing that the pleasure depended on distance from real loss.
options.why: It offers two explanations (P2–P3) and then the limiting condition of distance (P4).

options.text: showing that ruins are more beautiful than complete buildings.
options.why: The author explains a taste without ranking buildings.

options.text: arguing that eighteenth-century travelers were indifferent to suffering.
options.why: The author notes a limit to their taste, not general indifference.

options.text: tracing the history of the folly as an architectural form.
options.why: Follies are one detail in paragraph 1.

items.tldr: Two reasons ruins pleased, and one condition: distance.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 the taste. P2 flattery. P3 imagination. P4 the limit of distance.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: To explain the taste and its limits.

items.takeaway: Main-idea answers should include the author's turn ("but neither explains its limits").

items.prompt: As described in the passage, a "folly" was

options.text: a painting of a ruined abbey.
options.why: Painters depicted ruins, but a folly was a built structure.

options.text: a castle damaged in a recent war.
options.why: Recent damage is what travelers didn't find beautiful.

options.text: a building made to look partly destroyed from the start.
options.why: Paragraph 1 defines it as designed from the start to look half destroyed.

options.text: a ruin restored to its original condition.
options.why: A folly was built to look ruined, not restored.

items.tldr: A folly was a ruin built on purpose.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The last sentence of paragraph 1.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Designed from the start to look half destroyed.

items.takeaway: Definitions inside dashes or after "a" are prime material for detail questions.

items.prompt: The second explanation (paragraph 3) implies that a perfectly preserved ancient temple would be

options.text: less engaging to the viewer's imagination than the same temple in ruins.
options.why: A complete building tells its story fully, leaving no gaps for the viewer to fill.
Melancholy belongs to the first explanation and to ruins, not intact buildings.
On this view, ruins please because of their incompleteness.
Access isn't discussed.

items.tldr: No gaps means less for the imagination to do.

steps.label: The view
steps.body: Ruins please because the viewer fills in gaps.

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: A complete building leaves no gaps, so it engages the imagination less.

items.takeaway: To infer from a view, apply its reasoning to the new case.

items.prompt: The author mentions the ruined cottages of the poor (paragraph 4) primarily in order to

options.text: support the claim that ruins flatter the viewer.
options.why: The example points to a limit, not support for the first explanation.

options.text: argue that eighteenth-century travelers should have helped the poor.
options.why: The author makes no moral demand.

options.text: identify a limit to the taste for ruins that neither explanation accounts for.
options.why: Travelers didn't find these ruins beautiful, which neither flattery nor imagination explains.

options.text: give another example of a fashionable ruin.
options.why: These ruins were not found beautiful.

items.tldr: The cottages show that recent, nearby ruin didn't please.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "Both answers help explain the fashion, but neither explains its limits."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The cottages are the limiting case.

items.takeaway: Examples right after "but neither explains" mark the gap in the explanations.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following would most likely be enjoyed the way eighteenth-century travelers enjoyed ruins?

options.text: A neighborhood damaged by a hurricane last month
options.why: Recent destruction is still someone's loss.

options.text: The remains of a medieval fortress visited by tourists centuries after it was abandoned
options.why: Its destruction is old enough to be contemplated rather than suffered.

options.text: A family's home after a recent fire
options.why: The loss is recent and personal.

options.text: A cathedral that was completed last year
options.why: A complete new building isn't a ruin at all.

items.tldr: Old, distant ruin pleases; recent loss doesn't.

steps.label: Condition
steps.body: Destruction old or distant enough to be no one's loss.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The centuries-old fortress.

items.takeaway: Apply the author's limiting condition, not just the general taste.

items.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Morris wanted to abolish all machines.
options.why: His complaint "was not against machines as such."

options.text: Although Morris's movement could not make handmade goods affordable to workers, his critique of how work is organized remains relevant.
options.why: The passage acknowledges the contradiction (P2) and defends the lasting critique (P3–P4).

options.text: The movement's chief goal was to recreate a medieval past.
options.why: That is the critics' view, which the author calls too harsh.

options.text: The movement succeeded in making beautiful goods available to ordinary workers.
options.why: Workers could rarely afford the goods.

items.tldr: The movement failed on price, but its critique of work endures.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 the revolt. P2 the contradiction. P3 the deeper complaint. P4 the legacy.

steps.label: Main idea
steps.body: A practical failure with a lasting insight.

items.takeaway: Look for the author's balance of concession and defense.

items.prompt: According to the passage, the contradiction Morris recognized was that

options.why: The wealthy were the main buyers of handmade goods.

options.text: the workers the movement championed could rarely afford its products.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the buyers were mostly wealthy, not the workers.

options.text: craftsmen refused to use traditional methods.
options.why: Nothing suggests craftsmen rejected traditional methods.

options.text: machines produced more beautiful goods than craftsmen did.
options.why: The movement produced work of extraordinary beauty.

items.tldr: The makers couldn't afford what they made.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The end of paragraph 2.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Champions of workers, products for the wealthy.

items.takeaway: "Contradiction" questions usually point to two facts the passage sets side by side.

items.prompt: The author's response to the critics in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.text: prove that medieval workers were happier than factory workers.
options.why: The passage makes no claim about medieval workers' happiness.
Factories are mentioned only to describe what Morris objected to.

options.text: distinguish Morris's objection to the organization of work from a simple rejection of technology.
options.why: The author says Morris's complaint "did not depend on rejecting technology."

options.text: concede that the movement was mere nostalgia.
options.why: The author calls that judgment too harsh.

items.tldr: The real target was how work was organized, not machines.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "That judgment is too harsh. Morris's deeper complaint was not against machines as such..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It separates the critique from mere nostalgia or technophobia.

items.takeaway: "Too harsh" introduces a correction; the function is to refine, not to reject.

items.prompt: Which of the following modern practices would the author most likely regard as part of Morris's legacy?

options.text: A museum that displays medieval tools behind glass
options.why: The legacy concerns how work is organized, not preserving the past.

options.text: A store that sells mass-produced copies of antique chairs
options.why: Copying old styles isn't the legacy the author describes.

options.text: A factory that replaces its designers with software
options.why: That separates designing from making even further.

options.text: A furniture company whose designers work in the shop to learn how their designs are built
options.why: It reconnects design and making, as the author says the legacy does.

items.tldr: Designers who understand how things are made carry the legacy.

steps.label: The legacy
steps.body: Named makers, and designers who understand materials and methods.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Designers working in the shop.

items.takeaway: Application answers often mirror the author's own examples from the last paragraph.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward Morris is best described as

options.text: appreciative of his central insight, while acknowledging the movement's practical shortcomings.
options.why: The author grants the cost problem but defends the critique as lasting.
The author acknowledges the movement's contradiction.

options.text: dismissive of him as a nostalgic dreamer.
options.why: That is the critics' judgment, which the author rejects.
The author takes a position against the critics.

items.tldr: Admiring, with an honest note about cost.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The concession in P2 and the defense in P3–P4.

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Appreciative and balanced.

items.takeaway: Balanced passages call for balanced tone answers.

items.prompt: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

options.text: explain the chemical techniques used to remove varnish from old paintings.
options.why: The author says the dispute was less about chemistry than about what a restorer owes the work.

options.text: argue that restoration is an act of interpretation that should be carried out openly and with humility.
options.why: The last paragraph concludes that every removal is a judgment, so restorers should document their choices and accept later disagreement.

options.text: show that an artist's original intention can never be known.
options.why: The author says intention is rarely recoverable with certainty, not that it can never be known.

options.text: defend the restorers of the chapel frescoes against their critics.
options.why: The chapel is the opening example; the author never takes a side in that particular dispute.

items.tldr: Restoration is interpretation, so restorers should make their judgments visible and reversible.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 sets up the dispute. P2 and P3 give two answers and their limits. P4 says both are interpretive and describes responsible practice.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: The author's own position arrives in P4, and the answer must capture it.

items.takeaway: The primary purpose usually lives in the author's conclusion, not in the opening example.

items.prompt: The author mentions final glazes added over dry fresco (paragraph 2) primarily in order to

options.text: argue that frescoes should never be cleaned.
options.why: The author rejects mechanical rules in both directions and accepts some cleaning.

options.text: suggest that the chapel's painter was careless in his technique.
options.why: Nothing in the passage criticizes the painter's technique.

options.text: illustrate why a restorer guided by the artist's intention might mistakenly remove part of the original.
options.why: The glazes can look like dirt, so a restorer seeking the original may remove it, which is the difficulty the paragraph raises.

options.text: support the view that the darkening of a painting is part of its history.
options.why: That is the second answer, in paragraph 3. The glazes illustrate a problem for the first answer.

items.tldr: The glazes show how chasing the "original" can destroy it.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The glazes come right after "intention is rarely recoverable with certainty."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: They are the concrete case behind that difficulty.

items.takeaway: For function questions, read the sentence before the detail; the detail usually supports it.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree that a defender of patina

options.why: Documentation is the author's recommendation, and nothing suggests patina defenders oppose it.

options.text: would still accept removing some material from a painting's surface.
options.why: The author notes that few defenders of patina would leave a painting under soot that hides its figures.

options.text: considers the darkened colors to be what the artist intended.
options.why: The patina view values age as part of the object's life, not as the artist's intention.

options.text: believes the artist's intention is irrelevant to restoration.
options.why: The patina view stresses history; nothing says it treats intention as irrelevant.

items.tldr: Even patina's defenders would clean off soot, so they accept some removal.

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: So they accept removing at least some material.

items.takeaway: A supported inference sits one short step from a specific sentence.

items.prompt: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as responsible restoration?

options.text: A conservator follows a fixed protocol so that personal judgment never affects the result.
options.why: The author says the responsible restorer is not one who claims to have no point of view.

options.text: A conservator removes a later overpainting, records each step with photographs, and uses materials that can be taken off later.
options.why: This matches the author's ideal of documented, reversible choices.

options.text: A conservator refuses to remove soot because any intervention would erase the painting's history.
options.why: The author says even patina's defenders wouldn't leave figures buried under soot.

options.text: A conservator strips every surface layer down to the original plaster so that nothing later remains.
options.why: That applies the intention view mechanically and risks removing original glazes.

items.tldr: Responsible restoration means documented, reversible choices.

steps.label: Author's standard
steps.body: Document choices, keep them reversible, and accept that others may disagree.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only the photographed, reversible removal meets all three.

items.takeaway: Application answers should match the author's stated values, usually found in the conclusion.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the two answers described in paragraphs 2 and 3 is best described as

options.text: critical of each when applied rigidly, but appreciative of what they share.
options.why: The author shows each answer's limits, then says what they share matters more than what divides them.

options.text: firmly committed to the first and dismissive of the second.
options.why: The author points out a serious difficulty with the intention view.

options.text: firmly committed to the second and dismissive of the first.
options.why: The author says the patina view "has limits" too.

options.text: indifferent, since restoration is purely a matter of technique.
options.why: The author insists restoration is interpretation, not mere technique.

items.tldr: Each answer fails when applied mechanically, but both rightly treat restoration as interpretation.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "Neither answer... can be applied mechanically. What they share is more important than what divides them."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Mixed, critical of rigidity and appreciative of the shared insight.

items.takeaway: CARS authors often hold mixed attitudes. Be wary of answers that are wholly for or against.

items.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Recordings and films are the best way to restore an object's original context.
options.why: Paragraph 3 warns that such reconstructions can freeze a living tradition.

options.text: Preserving objects matters more than helping visitors understand them.
options.why: The author argues that display aims at understanding, which preservation alone can't justify.

options.text: Museums should return all ceremonial objects to their communities of origin.
options.why: The author proposes partnership over display, not wholesale return.

options.text: Because displaying an object implies it should be understood, museums should share decisions about presenting it with the communities that made it.
options.why: This links the argument of paragraph 2 to the author's recommendation in paragraph 4.

items.tldr: Display should aim at understanding, which requires partnering with the communities of origin.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 shows what labels leave out. P2 says preservation can't justify display. P3 flags the risk of reconstructions. P4 recommends partnership.

steps.label: Main idea
steps.body: The thread is understanding through partnership.

items.takeaway: The main idea connects the problem the author raises to the solution the author endorses.

items.prompt: The author's remark about climate-controlled vaults (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.text: support the curators' claim that removal from context is the price of preservation.
options.why: It undercuts that defense by showing it "proves too much."

options.text: illustrate how expensive preservation has become.
options.why: Cost is never discussed.

options.text: recommend that museums store fragile objects out of public view.
options.why: The vault is a thought experiment that exposes a weak argument, not a recommendation.

options.text: show that the preservation argument cannot, by itself, justify putting objects on display.
options.why: If preservation were the only goal, vaults would do; display must therefore aim at something more.

items.tldr: The vault example shows that preservation can't explain why objects are displayed.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The vault follows "the argument proves too much."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It shows that the preservation defense would justify vaults, not displays.

items.takeaway: "Proves too much" signals a reductio: the author follows an argument to a conclusion its defenders wouldn't accept.

items.prompt: The author's concern about reconstructed displays (paragraph 3) suggests that the author believes

options.text: curators deliberately misrepresent the cultures they study.
options.why: The author calls these efforts "well meant."

options.text: recordings of ceremonies are usually inaccurate.
options.why: The problem is freezing one version, not inaccuracy.

options.text: objects should be displayed without any accompanying information.
options.why: The author criticizes bare labels for failing to provide understanding.

options.text: the traditions associated with such objects have continued to change.
options.why: The worry is that a reconstruction freezes a living tradition, as if its makers had stopped changing.

items.tldr: Calling the tradition "living" implies it keeps changing.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: A reconstruction "can freeze a living tradition into a single 'authentic' version."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: That worry only makes sense if the tradition keeps changing.

items.takeaway: Ask what the author must believe for a stated worry to make sense.

items.prompt: Which of the following museum policies would the author most likely support?

options.text: Displaying each object alongside a reconstruction of its original ceremony.
options.why: The author warns that such reconstructions can freeze a living tradition.

options.text: Replacing short labels with longer ones written by the museum's own specialists.
options.why: More museum-authored text still leaves the museum alone settling the object's meaning.

options.text: Keeping ceremonial objects in storage so that visitors cannot misunderstand them.
options.why: The author wants understanding through conversation, not avoidance.

options.text: Asking representatives of a community whether a ceremonial object should be exhibited, and how.
options.why: That is the partnership the author recommends, including the choice not to show an object at all.

items.tldr: The author wants communities of origin to share decisions about display.

steps.label: Author's solution
steps.body: Treat communities of origin as partners who decide how, or whether, objects are shown.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only the consultation policy gives them that role.

items.takeaway: When the author proposes a solution, the best application usually enacts it directly.

items.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most challenge the author's claim that collaboration is "a more promising approach"?

options.text: Visitors to collaboratively designed exhibits understand the objects' original uses no better than visitors who see standard labels.
options.why: The author's case rests on display aiming at understanding; if collaboration doesn't improve understanding, its promise is in doubt.

options.text: Some communities of origin have asked museums to display their objects.
options.why: That fits the collaborative approach, since communities are deciding how objects are shown.

options.text: Collaborative exhibits take longer to plan than conventional ones.
options.why: The author already concedes that collaboration is slower.

options.text: Many museum visitors enjoy recordings and films of ceremonies.
options.why: Enjoyment of reconstructions says nothing about collaboration's value.

items.tldr: Collaboration's promise depends on better understanding; showing it doesn't help would undercut it.

steps.label: Find the support
steps.body: Display implies the object should be understood; collaboration replaces silence with conversation.

steps.label: Undercut it
steps.body: Evidence that collaboration doesn't improve understanding hits that support directly.

items.takeaway: Concessions the author already makes can't challenge the argument.

items.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.text: arguing that reading aloud is superior to reading silently.
options.why: The author compares the practices but never ranks them.

options.text: defending eighteenth-century moralists' warnings about novels.
options.why: The author calls much of their alarm condescension, while granting one real insight.

options.text: explaining how the novel and silent private reading developed together, and what kind of community resulted.
options.why: The passage traces the link between form and practice (P1–P2), the critics' response (P3) and the new public (P4).

options.text: showing that novels were read mainly by young women.
options.why: Young women appear only in the critics' warnings.

items.tldr: The novel and private reading grew up together, and together they created a dispersed public.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 private reading is new. P2 the novel suits it. P3 critics saw its independence. P4 it created a new public.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: The passage explains a historical development and its result.

items.takeaway: Pick the answer that covers every paragraph's contribution, not just one.

items.prompt: According to the passage, letters and diaries suited the eighteenth-century novel because they

options.text: invited a reader to linger over a character's private thoughts.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says such material suited a reader who could linger, reread and imagine another's inner life.

options.text: were easy to perform aloud before an audience.
options.why: The passage says such material is awkward to perform before an audience.

options.text: allowed authors to conceal their own identities.
options.why: Authorial anonymity isn't discussed.

options.text: were the most common forms of writing at the time.
options.why: The passage never compares how common different forms were.

items.tldr: Private documents suited a reader who could linger over inner life.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: Such material is "perfectly suited to a reader who can linger, reread and imagine herself into another person's inner life."

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Lingering over private thoughts is the stated reason.

items.takeaway: Detail questions reward the paraphrase closest to the passage's own words.

items.prompt: The author calls the novel's critics "among its most perceptive readers" in order to

options.text: suggest that the critics secretly enjoyed reading novels.
options.why: The phrase is figurative. The critics understood the novel's effect; nothing says they enjoyed it.

options.text: show that the critics wrote better novels than the authors they attacked.
options.why: The passage never mentions novels written by the critics.

options.text: endorse the critics' warnings about idleness and unrealistic expectations.
options.why: The author dismisses much of that alarm as condescension.

options.text: acknowledge that the critics correctly saw that private reading escaped social supervision, even though their alarm was condescending.
options.why: The sentence follows the concession that critics "noticed something real" about readers beyond supervision.

items.tldr: The critics misjudged the stakes but understood the novel's power to escape supervision.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "But the critics noticed something real..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The phrase credits that insight while the author keeps rejecting their condescension.

items.takeaway: A "But" after a criticism usually introduces a partial concession; the function answer keeps both halves.

items.prompt: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the "new kind of public" described in paragraph 4?

options.text: It discouraged readers from forming their own opinions.
options.why: Readers argued about characters, which shows independent opinions.

options.text: It was limited to members of formal reading societies.
options.why: Letters and periodicals also linked readers, not only societies.

options.text: It replaced families and churches as the main source of moral guidance.
options.why: The passage claims nothing about moral guidance shifting to readers.

options.text: Its members did not need to be gathered in one place to share an experience.
options.why: The author contrasts it with "a crowd gathered in one place" and calls it a dispersed community.

items.tldr: The new public was dispersed, linked by shared reading rather than by place.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: "Not a crowd gathered in one place, but a dispersed community..."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: Shared experience without physical gathering.

items.takeaway: Contrasts the author draws ("not X but Y") are prime material for inference answers.

items.prompt: Which of the following is most analogous to the "new kind of public" the author describes?

options.text: A student reading a textbook alone for an exam
options.why: That is solitary reading with no community at all.

options.text: Viewers in many cities discussing the same television series in online forums
options.why: A dispersed group linked by a shared imaginative experience, as with the novel's readers.

options.text: A crowd gathered in a theater to watch a play
options.why: That is a crowd in one place, the contrast case.

options.text: A family reading a story aloud together at bedtime
options.why: That resembles the older, social reading the passage contrasts with the novel.

items.tldr: Dispersed people linked by a shared story match the novel's public.

steps.label: Abstract it
steps.body: Separate individuals, the same imaginative work, ongoing discussion.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Online fans of one series fit all three features.

items.takeaway: For analogies, list the defining features first, then check each answer against all of them.

items.prompt: Which of the following best states the author's position?

options.text: Our ordinary judgments are sound, so the control principle should be abandoned.
options.why: The author keeps the control principle for blame.

options.text: Luck should not affect how we judge a person's character, but it can affect what that person owes to others.
options.why: That is the closing distinction between blame and responsibility.

options.text: People should be blamed for outcomes rather than for their choices.
options.why: The author says blame should track only what a person controlled.

options.text: The two drivers deserve exactly the same treatment in every respect.
options.why: That is the "bite the bullet" view, which the author finds too costly.

items.tldr: Luck changes what we owe, not who we are.

steps.label: Find the thesis
steps.body: "A better response, I suggest, distinguishes blame from responsibility."

steps.label: State it
steps.body: Blame follows control; responsibility to victims can follow outcomes.

items.takeaway: "I suggest" and "a better response" flag the author's own view.

items.prompt: The examples of the rescuers and the attempted murderer (paragraph 2) are offered mainly to

options.text: show that judgments shaped by outcomes are widespread, not limited to the case of the drivers.
options.why: They come right after "our actual judgments rarely respect this principle" and generalize the puzzle.

options.text: suggest that the law punishes failed attempts too harshly.
options.why: The passage notes that attempts are condemned less, not too harshly.

options.text: prove that the control principle is false.
options.why: The author presents a dilemma: either the principle or the judgments must give way.

options.text: illustrate the author's distinction between blame and responsibility.
options.why: That distinction comes later, in paragraph 4.

items.tldr: More examples show the puzzle is general.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: They follow "our actual judgments rarely respect this principle."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: They show that outcome-based judgment is common.

items.takeaway: Examples right after a general claim usually exist to support or extend it.

items.prompt: The author's objection to the "bite the bullet" response relies on the assumption that

options.text: consistency is not a virtue in moral theory.
options.why: The author grants that the view "has the virtue of consistency."

options.text: emotions are always a reliable guide to moral truth.
options.why: The objection needs only this one feeling to be warranted, not all emotions.

options.text: the remorse felt by people who have caused harm is not simply a mistake.
options.why: The objection is that the view makes such remorse "a kind of confusion," which the author treats as unacceptable.

options.text: the second driver was more reckless than the first.
options.why: The passage stipulates that the drivers were equally careless.

items.tldr: The objection works only if the harmful driver's remorse is fitting, not confused.

steps.label: The objection
steps.body: The view implies the second driver's anguish is confusion; few who have caused harm would accept that.

steps.label: Assumption
steps.body: Their remorse is appropriate.

items.takeaway: To find an assumption, ask what must be true for the author's objection to land.

items.prompt: On the author's view, what is the moral status of the first driver, who arrived home safely?

options.text: He is as much at fault as the second driver, though he owes no one repair.
options.why: Blame tracks control, which was the same for both; owing repair follows outcomes, and he harmed no one.

options.text: He deserves no blame, since his recklessness harmed no one.
options.why: The author says the drivers are "equally at fault."

options.text: He owes the child's family an apology as well.
options.why: Only the driver whose recklessness "landed on someone" owes the family.

options.text: He deserves more blame than the second driver for escaping the consequences.
options.why: Nothing in the passage suggests blame increases for escaping consequences.

items.tldr: Equal blame, but nothing owed, because his recklessness harmed no one.

steps.label: Blame
steps.body: Same control, so the same fault.

steps.label: Responsibility
steps.body: No victim, so no debt of apology or repair.

items.takeaway: Apply both halves of an author's distinction separately.

items.prompt: As used in paragraph 3, "bite the bullet" most nearly means

options.text: refuse to take any position on the puzzle
options.why: The response takes a firm position.
That is the literal sense, not the meaning in this philosophical context.

options.text: accept an unwelcome implication for the sake of consistency
options.why: The view accepts that the drivers are equally blameworthy despite our reactions, gaining consistency at a cost.

options.text: give up the control principle under pressure
options.why: Biting the bullet here keeps the control principle and rejects our judgments.

items.tldr: Here it means accepting a hard consequence to stay consistent.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: The response keeps the principle and says our differing reactions are mere emotion.

steps.label: Meaning
steps.body: It accepts an uncomfortable implication rather than abandoning the principle.

items.takeaway: For meaning-in-context questions, ignore the dictionary sense and read the surrounding sentences.

items.prompt: The main point of the passage is that

options.text: although the revival's ideal of untouched music didn't match reality, authenticity can be understood as a serious relationship to a tradition.
options.why: The passage exposes the ideal's ironies (P2), resists dismissing it (P3), and redefines it (P4).

options.text: folk songs recorded before radio are more authentic than later versions.
options.why: The author locates authenticity in a performer's relationship to a tradition, not in the age of a recording.

options.text: rural singers deliberately deceived the collectors who recorded them.
options.why: It was the collectors who left popular songs off their tapes.

options.text: the folk revival was a commercial scheme disguised as preservation.
options.why: The author credits the revival with real benefits for musicians and songs.

items.tldr: The purity ideal was flawed, but authenticity survives as careful attention to a tradition.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 the ideal. P2 its ironies. P3 not a mere myth. P4 a better definition.

steps.label: Main point
steps.body: The redefinition in P4, set against the ironies in P2.

items.takeaway: When a passage criticizes an idea and then rescues it, the main point is usually the rescued version.

items.prompt: The author suggests that the collectors' recordings of rural singers were

options.text: incomplete records of what those singers actually performed.
options.why: Collectors "quietly left off" the popular songs that singers had absorbed from radio.
The recordings became commercial records, and the singers had absorbed radio songs.
The recordings were pressed into records and widely learned from.

options.text: the main reason rural singers stopped performing.
options.why: The passage says the revival sometimes gave such singers new audiences.

items.tldr: Leaving popular songs off the tapes made the recordings selective.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: Popular songs were "a mixture the collectors often quietly left off their tapes."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: The tapes didn't show the singers' full repertoire.

items.takeaway: Words like "quietly left off" carry the inference; slow down on them.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3?

options.text: It summarizes the history of the recording industry.
options.why: The recording industry appears only as part of the revival's ironies.

options.text: It cautions against dismissing authenticity entirely by pointing to the revival's real benefits.
options.why: It calls the "myth" conclusion "too quick" and lists real effects.

options.text: It introduces a new criticism of the folk revival.
options.why: It defends the revival's effects rather than criticizing it.

options.text: It provides evidence that authenticity was only a myth.
options.why: It rejects that conclusion.

items.tldr: Paragraph 3 blocks the too-quick conclusion that authenticity was a myth.

steps.label: Signal
steps.body: "But that conclusion is too quick."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It turns the argument from criticism toward a more balanced view.

items.takeaway: "That conclusion is too quick" marks a turn; the paragraph pushes back on what came before.

items.prompt: Which of the following performers would the author most likely regard as having a genuine relationship to a tradition?

options.text: A band that rearranges traditional songs to sound like current hits in order to sell more records
options.why: Nothing here shows the serious attention to a tradition that the author values.

options.text: A performer who refuses to sing any song he has heard on a record
options.why: The author rejects purity of sources as the measure of authenticity.

options.text: A singer who performs songs learned from her grandmother without any interest in where they came from
options.why: A pure source sung "by rote" is exactly what the author ranks lower.

options.text: A guitarist who learned old blues songs from records, researched the musicians who first sang them, and performs them with care
options.why: Learning from records, studying history and performing with care is the author's own example of genuine relation.

items.tldr: Serious attention, not a pure source, makes a relationship to a tradition genuine.

steps.label: Author's standard
steps.body: Authenticity is a relationship marked by study and care.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The guitarist matches the author's own example almost exactly.

items.takeaway: When the author gives an example of the ideal, the right application usually mirrors it.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the musicians of the folk revival is best described as

options.why: The author highlights the revival's contradictions.
The author argues for a redefinition of authenticity.

options.text: appreciative of the best musicians' care, while skeptical of the revival's ideal of purity
options.why: The author admires the "seriousness of their attention" but exposes the ironies of the purity ideal.
The author points out ironies but also credits the revival's real benefits.

items.tldr: Mixed, admiring the attention and doubting the purity ideal.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "The irony is..." and "What made the revival's best musicians admirable..."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Critical of the ideal, appreciative of the best practitioners.

items.takeaway: Extreme tone answers (contempt, uncritical praise) are rarely right in CARS.

items.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Modern Hebrew is the only language that has ever been revived.
options.why: The author mentions revivals under way from Wales to New Zealand.

options.text: Linguists' documentation is enough to save an endangered language.
options.why: The author says revitalization succeeds when families choose the language, not when grammars are documented.

options.text: Languages are lost through speakers' everyday choices, and for the same reason they can be revived when communities choose to speak them again.
options.why: This joins the quiet loss (P1) with the closing claim that a language lives in its speakers' decisions (P4).

options.text: Endangered languages, like extinct species, can never be recovered.
options.why: The author says a language, unlike a species, can return.

items.tldr: Choices lose languages, and choices can bring them back.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 quiet loss. P2 the biological metaphor's truth. P3 its limit. P4 choice is the heart of it.

steps.label: Main idea
steps.body: The theme of choice, which explains both loss and recovery.

items.takeaway: When a passage's last sentence says "both why… and why…", it is often the main idea.

items.prompt: According to the passage, most languages that disappear do so because

options.why: The passage never mentions bans.

options.text: natural disasters wipe out their speakers.
options.why: The author says most will not disappear in a dramatic event.

options.text: parents raise their children in a language that seems more useful.
options.why: Paragraph 1 describes this quiet shift as the usual path.
Linguists' attention isn't given as a cause.

items.tldr: Parents choosing a more useful language for their children.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The middle of paragraph 1.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Children raised in a more useful language.

items.takeaway: Detail answers restate the passage; extreme causes it rules out are traps.

items.prompt: The author discusses Modern Hebrew primarily in order to

options.text: explain where the biological metaphor came from.
options.why: Hebrew is evidence against the metaphor's implication, not its origin.

options.text: argue that every endangered language should be revived.
options.why: The author says communities can choose to; no universal prescription is made.

options.text: illustrate that a language, unlike a species, can return after falling out of everyday use.
options.why: It is offered as the most famous case right after "A language can."

options.text: show that religious languages last longer than others.
options.why: The point is revival, not religious use.

items.tldr: Hebrew is the proof that languages can come back.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "A species, once extinct, cannot return. A language can. Modern Hebrew..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The key example for the author's counterpoint.

items.takeaway: Examples that follow a short, bold claim usually exist to prove it.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward comparing languages to biological species is best described as

options.why: The author points out where the metaphor misleads.

options.text: partly approving, since it captures a real loss, but wary of its suggestion that the loss is final.
options.why: The author says the comparison "captures something real" but "can mislead."
The author spends two paragraphs evaluating it.

options.text: dismissive, since the comparison captures nothing true.
options.why: The author grants that it captures something real.

items.tldr: Useful metaphor, misleading in one key way.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "The comparison captures something real." Then: "But the biological metaphor can mislead."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Mixed: partial approval with a warning.

items.takeaway: A paragraph of credit followed by "But" signals a mixed attitude.

items.prompt: Which of the following would the author most likely consider the strongest sign that a revitalization effort is succeeding?

options.text: Young parents in the community choosing to speak the language to their children at home
options.why: The author says revitalization succeeds when families use the language at home.

options.text: A linguist publishing a complete dictionary of the language
options.why: The author says documentation alone isn't success.

options.text: Recordings of elders stored in a university archive
options.why: Recordings help a language persist, but success requires everyday use.

options.text: A museum exhibit about the language's history
options.why: An exhibit preserves memory but doesn't make the language a language of daily life.

items.tldr: Home use by families is the author's measure of success.

steps.label: Criterion
steps.body: Families use the language at home; children hear it daily.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Parents speaking it to their children.

items.takeaway: Application answers should meet the author's stated criterion exactly.

items.prompt: The central thesis of the passage is that

options.text: societies of the Pacific Northwest valued trade more than gifts.
options.why: The passage makes no such comparison.

options.text: Mauss proved that generosity is a disguised form of self-interest.
options.why: The author calls this cynical reading a misreading.

options.text: gifts create binding obligations that make them social rather than insincere, and those obligations persist alongside market exchange.
options.why: It joins Mauss's finding (P1–P2), the author's reading of it (P3) and the modern situation (P4).

options.text: gift-giving disappeared with the rise of markets.
options.why: The author says markets confined these obligations, not abolished them.

items.tldr: Gifts bind people together, and they still do in the spaces markets leave.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 gifts create obligations. P2 how binding they were. P3 social, not cynical. P4 confined but alive today.

steps.label: Thesis
steps.body: Obligation makes the gift social, then and now.

items.takeaway: When the author corrects a likely misreading, include the correction in the main idea.

items.prompt: According to the passage, rival leaders in some societies gained prestige by

options.why: Refusing a gift could be an insult; it isn't described as a route to prestige.

options.text: giving away or destroying goods to place others in their debt.
options.why: Paragraph 2 describes exactly this competition.

options.text: writing down the obligations others owed them.
options.why: The obligations were not written down.
Profit-making isn't mentioned.

items.tldr: Prestige came from making others indebted.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The third sentence of paragraph 2.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Giving away or destroying goods.

items.takeaway: Watch for answers that twist a nearby detail, like refusing gifts.

items.prompt: The author's discussion of a "cynical" reading of Mauss (paragraph 3) serves mainly to

options.text: head off a misinterpretation of Mauss's argument.
options.why: The author says that reading "misses his point" and restates what Mauss meant.

options.text: endorse the views of Mauss's critics.
options.why: The author rejects the cynical reading.

options.text: concede that gifts are usually insincere.
options.why: The author says the obligations make gifts social, not insincere.
No new evidence appears in paragraph 3.

items.tldr: The paragraph blocks the cynical reading.

steps.label: Signal
steps.body: "That reading misses his point."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: A correction of a tempting interpretation.

items.takeaway: "It would be easy to read X as..." almost always sets up a correction.

items.prompt: The author suggests that a typical market purchase differs from a gift in that the purchase

options.text: is always worth more than a gift.
options.why: Value isn't compared.

options.text: creates stronger obligations between the parties.
options.why: A purchase, once paid, is finished.

options.text: requires the seller to give something back later.
options.why: The point is that nothing further is owed.

options.text: is designed to leave no lasting bond between buyer and seller.
options.why: Paragraph 4 describes transactions "designed to leave no bond behind."

items.tldr: A purchase ends the relationship; a gift starts one.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: "...transactions designed to leave no bond behind."

steps.label: Infer

items.prompt: Every time Maya cleans her room, her parents stop the daily reminders she finds annoying. Over the next month, Maya cleans her room more often. Which process best explains this change?

options.why: Removing an unpleasant stimulus (the reminders) makes the behavior more frequent.
Classical conditioning pairs two stimuli. This is about the consequences of a voluntary behavior, which is operant conditioning.
Punishment makes a behavior less frequent. Maya cleans more.
Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant. Here something unpleasant is removed.

items.tldr: The reminders (unpleasant) are removed when she cleans, so cleaning increases. That's negative reinforcement.

steps.label: Direction
steps.body: The behavior becomes more frequent, so it's reinforcement.

steps.label: Add or remove
steps.body: Something unpleasant is taken away, so it's negative.

items.takeaway: Reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases it. Positive adds a stimulus; negative removes one.

items.prompt: When a coworker arrives late, Jordan concludes that the coworker is irresponsible. When Jordan arrives late, Jordan blames the traffic. This pattern best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: That's the belief that people get what they deserve.
Confirmation bias is seeking evidence for what you already believe.
That covers only the half about judging the coworker. The question describes the self–other contrast.
Jordan explains others' behavior by disposition and Jordan's own by situation. That contrast defines the actor–observer bias.

items.tldr: Their lateness is character, my lateness is traffic. That self–other split is the actor–observer bias.

steps.label: Others
steps.body: The coworker's lateness is blamed on disposition ("irresponsible").

steps.label: Self
steps.body: Jordan's own lateness is blamed on the situation ("traffic").

steps.label: Name
steps.body: Different attributions for the same behavior depending on who does it is actor–observer bias.

items.takeaway: The fundamental attribution error is about judging others. The actor–observer bias is the contrast between how we judge others and ourselves.

items.prompt: A survey of 2,000 college students finds that students who sleep more hours per night tend to have higher GPAs. Which conclusion is best supported by this finding?

options.text: Sleep duration and GPA are associated, but the survey cannot show which, if either, causes the other.
options.why: Correlational data support an association only. Confounders like workload could drive both.

options.text: Getting more sleep causes students' GPAs to rise.
options.why: A survey shows an association, not cause and effect.

options.text: Earning a higher GPA causes students to sleep more.
options.why: Reversing the direction is still a causal claim the survey can't support.

options.text: Sleep duration and GPA are unrelated in the general population.
options.why: The survey found a relationship. It just can't explain it.

items.tldr: A correlation shows the two go together, not that one causes the other.

steps.label: Design
steps.body: A survey measures variables without manipulating them. It's correlational.

steps.label: Limit
steps.body: It can't rule out reverse causation or confounders (stress, workload, health).

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only the association claim is supported.

items.takeaway: Correlational studies support associations, not causal direction.

items.prompt: A sociologist argues that schools persist because they sort people into occupations and pass on shared values, helping society function smoothly. This argument most closely reflects which perspective?

options.why: Social constructionism asks how shared meanings create social reality.
Conflict theory would say schools reproduce inequality and serve powerful groups.
Symbolic interactionism looks at everyday meanings and face-to-face interaction.
Functionalism explains institutions by the stabilizing functions they serve.

items.tldr: Explaining an institution by the functions that keep society stable is functionalism.

steps.label: Key words
steps.body: "Sort people," "pass on shared values," "function smoothly": all about stability and roles.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: That's the functionalist lens. Conflict theory would focus on inequality instead.

items.takeaway: Functionalism asks what an institution does for social stability. Conflict theory asks whom it benefits.

items.prompt: Students who study vocabulary in the same room where they later take the test recall more words than students who study somewhere else. This finding best illustrates

options.why: That's old learning disrupting new learning.
That's about matching internal states, like mood or alertness, not the room.
Matching the physical setting at study and test provides retrieval cues.
That's about remembering items at the start and end of a list.

items.tldr: Same room at study and test means better retrieval cues. That's context-dependent memory.

steps.label: Spot the variable
steps.body: The only difference is the physical setting of study versus test.

steps.label: Name it
steps.body: External setting matching is context-dependent memory, an example of encoding specificity.

items.takeaway: External setting: context-dependent. Internal state: state-dependent.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old insists that a tall, thin glass holds more juice than a short, wide glass, even after watching the same juice poured from one to the other. According to Piaget, the child has not yet mastered

options.why: Understanding that quantity stays the same when shape changes develops in the concrete operational stage.
That develops in infancy (sensorimotor stage), long before age 4.
That belongs to the formal operational stage, but this task doesn't require it.
Attachment comes from a different theory and isn't about quantities.

items.tldr: Judging amount by height means the child lacks conservation, which is typical before about age 7.

steps.label: Stage
steps.body: A 4-year-old is in Piaget's preoperational stage.

steps.label: Skill
steps.body: Conservation, knowing amount doesn't change with shape, arrives in the concrete operational stage.

items.takeaway: Piaget's order: sensorimotor (object permanence), preoperational, concrete operational (conservation), formal operational (abstract thought).

items.prompt: After paying for an expensive gym membership she rarely uses, Dana convinces herself that the membership was worth it because the gym has a great sauna. This is best explained by

options.why: That's about performing differently in front of others.
That's about people failing to help when others are present.
That's liking something more through repeated exposure. She rarely goes.
She changes her belief about the membership to fit her costly choice.

items.tldr: She justifies a costly choice by changing her belief, which is how dissonance gets reduced.

steps.label: Conflict
steps.body: "I paid a lot" clashes with "I rarely use it."

steps.label: Resolution
steps.body: She adjusts her belief ("it's worth it for the sauna") to reduce the discomfort.

items.takeaway: Cognitive dissonance is resolved by changing beliefs or behavior. Effort justification is the classic example.
