passages.title: Gardens as arguments
paragraphs: A garden can look like the most innocent of human works: a place to walk, to sit, to grow food or flowers. Yet the great gardens of Europe were also arguments, laid out in soil and water, about the proper relation between human beings and the natural world.

The formal gardens of seventeenth-century France made their case through geometry. Long straight avenues ran to the horizon; hedges were clipped into walls and cones; water was forced upward in fountains or held still in rectangular pools. Every element announced that nature had been brought to order by human reason and, not incidentally, by the power of the king whose palace commanded the view. To walk in such a garden was to be reminded at every turn of where authority lay.

In eighteenth-century England, a different argument took root. Landscape gardeners removed straight lines, softened the edges of lakes and planted trees in irregular clumps, so that an estate seemed to roll naturally toward the horizon. The style was praised as a liberation of nature from tyranny, and admirers connected it with English political liberty. But the "natural" landscape was no less a construction than the formal garden. Hills were raised, rivers rerouted and, in some cases, whole villages moved out of the view so that the owner might look across an unbroken expanse.

Seen this way, the contest between the two styles was less a contest between art and nature than one between two ways of displaying power. The formal garden showed its control openly; the landscape garden concealed it behind an appearance of effortless freedom. Which is more honest is a question worth asking of more than gardens.

passages.title: The art of trying
paragraphs: When Michel de Montaigne published the first books of his Essais in 1580, he gave a new name to a new kind of writing. The French word essai means a trial or an attempt, and Montaigne's chapters are just that: attempts to think through a subject, whether friendship, cruelty, idleness or the education of children, without knowing in advance where the thinking will end. He announced in his preface that he himself was the matter of his book.

To a modern reader the confession sounds harmless, even charming. In its time it was close to scandalous. Serious books were expected to concern serious things: God, law, the deeds of great men. A minor nobleman examining his own habits, his kidney stones and his changing opinions seemed to waste the reader's time. Yet Montaigne's self-examination was not vanity. He studied himself because he was the one specimen of humanity he could observe from the inside, and he found that specimen inconsistent, changeable and often unsure.

That discovery shaped the form. An essay by Montaigne rarely proceeds in a straight line. It starts with one topic, wanders through quotations and anecdotes, contradicts an earlier claim, and sometimes ends far from where it began. Critics have called this disorder. It is better described as fidelity: a mind that changes as it thinks is rendered faithfully only by a prose that changes too.

The essay's later history has not always honored this origin. In schools, the essay became a tool of demonstration, a thesis stated in the first paragraph and proved in the next three, which is precisely the kind of foreknown argument Montaigne set out to avoid. There is nothing wrong with a well-organized argument. But to call it an essay is to forget that the form began as a way of finding out what one thinks, not of announcing it.

passages.title: The road with cannonballs
paragraphs: In 1855, during the Crimean War, the British photographer Roger Fenton made two photographs of the same stretch of road in a ravine that soldiers called the Valley of the Shadow of Death. In one, the road is scattered with cannonballs. In the other, the cannonballs lie in the ditch beside it. Ever since the two images were compared, people have argued about which came first, and therefore about whether Fenton moved the cannonballs onto the road to make a more dramatic picture.

The argument matters because of a belief that has followed photography from its beginning: that a photograph, unlike a painting, is a trace of the world rather than an interpretation of it. A painter can add a cannonball with a stroke of the brush; a camera, the reasoning goes, can record only what is there. If Fenton arranged the scene, he seems to have betrayed the medium's special promise.

Yet every photograph involves choices. The photographer decides where to stand, when to open the shutter, what to include at the edges of the frame and what to leave outside it. Fenton's bulky equipment and long exposures made truly spontaneous pictures impossible; nearly everything he photographed had to hold still. The line between selecting a scene and arranging one is less sharp than the controversy implies.

This does not mean that nothing was at stake. A viewer who believes the cannonballs fell where they lie learns something about the danger of that road; a viewer who learns they were placed there learns something different. The ethics of the photograph depend less on whether choices were made, since they always are, than on what the photograph leads its viewers to believe, and whether that belief is true.

passages.title: The pleasure of ruins
paragraphs: In the eighteenth century, European travelers developed a taste that would have puzzled many of their ancestors: they found ruins beautiful. Crumbling abbeys, broken columns and overgrown castles, once seen as signs of neglect or divine judgment, became destinations. Painters made careers of them, and wealthy landowners who lacked a real ruin sometimes built one, a "folly" designed from the start to look half destroyed.

Why should decay give pleasure? One answer is that ruins flatter the viewer. To stand before the fallen walls of a once-mighty building is to feel the passage of time while remaining, for the moment, outside it; the observer survives what the empire did not. The melancholy is real, but it is a comfortable melancholy, enjoyed at a safe distance.

A second answer looks to the imagination. A complete building tells its story fully; a ruin leaves gaps that the viewer fills in. The missing roof invites one to picture the hall it covered, and the vanished town invites one to people the empty field. Ruins, on this view, please not despite their incompleteness but because of it: they make the viewer a collaborator.

Both answers help explain the fashion, but neither explains its limits. The same travelers who sighed over Roman stones rarely found beauty in the ruined cottages of the poor around them, or in the damage of recent wars. Distance seems to be essential. A ruin pleases when its destruction is old enough, or far enough away, to be contemplated rather than suffered; when, in other words, it has ceased to be anyone's loss.

passages.title: Made by hand
paragraphs: In the second half of the nineteenth century, the English designer William Morris led a revolt against the products of the factory. Machine-made furniture, wallpaper and textiles, he argued, were cheap in every sense: poorly designed, carelessly made and produced by workers who took no pleasure in their labor. Against them Morris set the ideal of the craftsman, who designed and made an object from start to finish and could take pride in the result.

The movement Morris inspired produced work of extraordinary beauty, including hand-printed fabrics, carved chairs and finely printed books, and it changed the way many people thought about the objects in their homes. It also ran into a contradiction that Morris himself recognized. Handmade goods took far longer to produce than machine-made ones, and so they cost far more. The workers whose dignity the movement championed could rarely afford what they made; the buyers were mostly the wealthy.

Some critics conclude that the movement was simply nostalgic, a fantasy of a medieval past that never existed. That judgment is too harsh. Morris's deeper complaint was not against machines as such but against a way of organizing work that separated the people who designed things from the people who made them, and that treated workers as parts of a mechanism. That complaint did not depend on rejecting technology, and it has outlived the movement.

Its legacy is visible today wherever people seek out the work of named makers, or wherever designers insist on understanding the materials and methods by which their designs will be produced. The question Morris raised, whether work can be organized so that those who do it share in its meaning, remains unanswered, but it has not gone away.

passages.title: Cleaning the past
paragraphs: When the frescoes of a famous chapel were cleaned late in the twentieth century, many viewers were startled. Colors they had known as somber browns and smoky greens emerged as vivid oranges, pinks and acid yellows. Some critics accused the restorers of destroying the work; others insisted that, for the first time in centuries, the paintings could be seen as their maker intended. The dispute was less about chemistry than about what a restorer owes to a work of art.

One answer holds that the restorer owes everything to the artist's original intention. On this view, grime, varnish and later retouching are accretions that stand between us and the work, and the restorer's task is to remove them. The difficulty is that intention is rarely recoverable with certainty. Painters sometimes added final glazes over dry fresco, and these delicate layers can be indistinguishable from later dirt. A restorer confident that she is uncovering the original may in fact be removing it.

A second answer holds that the restorer owes something to history. An old painting is not only the product of a single moment of making; it is also an object that has lived through centuries, and the darkening of its surface is part of that life. To strip away every trace of age, this view suggests, is to replace a historical object with a modern reconstruction of what the past supposedly looked like. Yet this position, too, has limits. Few defenders of patina would leave a painting under a layer of candle soot that hides its figures entirely.

Neither answer, I think, can be applied mechanically. What they share is more important than what divides them: both treat restoration as interpretation rather than mere technique. Every decision about what to remove expresses a judgment about what the work is. The responsible restorer is therefore not the one who claims to have no point of view, but the one who documents her choices, keeps them reversible where possible, and accepts that a future generation may judge differently.

passages.title: The museum's silence
paragraphs: A carved wooden mask from West Africa hangs in a glass case in a European museum. A small label gives its region, its approximate date and the name of the collector who acquired it. What the label cannot convey is that the mask was made to be worn, in motion, at night, by a dancer whose identity it concealed, before an audience that knew what the performance meant. In the case, the mask is silent and still. The museum has preserved the object while removing nearly everything that made it significant to the people who made it.

Curators have long defended this practice on the grounds that removal from context is the price of preservation. Wooden masks decay; ceremonies change; a museum keeps an object safe for future generations. There is truth in this, but the argument proves too much. If preservation alone were the goal, a museum could keep its objects in climate-controlled vaults rather than display them. Display implies that the object is meant to be understood, and understanding is precisely what the bare label fails to provide.

Some museums have responded by reconstructing context: playing recordings of music, projecting films of ceremonies, or arranging objects as they might appear in use. These efforts are well meant but carry their own risk. A reconstruction chosen by curators thousands of miles away can freeze a living tradition into a single "authentic" version, as though the communities that made the objects had stopped changing when the collector left.

A more promising approach treats the communities of origin not as sources of information but as partners. When a museum invites members of those communities to decide how an object should be shown, or whether it should be shown at all, it acknowledges that the meaning of the object is not the museum's to settle. Such collaboration is slower and less predictable than writing a label. But it replaces the museum's silence with a conversation, which is what an object made for performance has always required.

passages.title: Reading alone
paragraphs: For most of history, reading was a social act. Texts were read aloud, in households, in churches, in taverns, so that a single literate person could share a book with many listeners. The silent, solitary reader absorbed in a novel, so familiar to us that she seems natural, is a comparatively recent figure, and the novel itself grew up alongside her.

The connection is not accidental. Novels of the eighteenth century specialized in the representation of private thought: letters never meant to be seen by anyone but their recipient, diaries, the unspoken reflections of a heroine alone in her room. Such material is awkward to perform before an audience, but perfectly suited to a reader who can linger, reread and imagine herself into another person's inner life. The form and the practice reinforced each other.

Contemporaries were not uniformly pleased. Moralists warned that novel reading, especially by young women, encouraged idleness, unrealistic expectations of love and a dangerous independence of mind. Much of this alarm now reads as condescension. But the critics noticed something real: a reader alone with a book was beyond the supervision of family and church in a way that a listener in a crowded room was not. The novel's critics were, in a sense, among its most perceptive readers.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that private reading cut readers off from community. Readers of novels wrote to authors, argued about characters in letters and periodicals, and formed reading societies that met to discuss the latest books. Private reading created a new kind of public: not a crowd gathered in one place, but a dispersed community linked by shared imaginative experience. That public, rather than the solitary reader, may be the novel's most lasting invention.

passages.title: Luck and blame
paragraphs: Two drivers leave the same party, each having had one drink too many. Both drive home carelessly along the same road. One arrives safely. The other, through no greater fault of his own, strikes a child who runs into the street. We blame the second driver far more severely than the first, and the law punishes him far more severely, too. Yet the difference between them seems to lie entirely in luck: in the timing of a child's dash across the road, which neither driver controlled.

Philosophers call this phenomenon moral luck, and it poses a genuine puzzle. Most of us accept, on reflection, that people should be judged only for what is within their control. But our actual judgments rarely respect this principle. We praise the rescuer whose dive succeeds more than the equally brave one whose dive fails; we condemn the attempted murderer less than the successful one. If the control principle is right, these judgments are mistaken. If the judgments are right, the principle must be wrong.

One response is to bite the bullet: the two drivers are equally blameworthy, and any difference in our reactions reflects mere emotion. This view has the virtue of consistency, but it has a cost. It implies that the second driver has no special reason to feel remorse toward the child's family, and that his anguish, however natural, is a kind of confusion. Few people who have caused real harm would accept that description of their own experience.

A better response, I suggest, distinguishes blame from responsibility. Blame, as a verdict on a person's character, should track only what the person controlled; in that sense the drivers are equally at fault. But responsibility, in the sense of owing something to those one has harmed, can follow outcomes. The second driver owes the child's family an apology, an accounting and perhaps repair, not because he is a worse person than the first, but because his recklessness, unlike the other's, landed on someone. Luck, on this view, does not change who we are; it changes what we owe.

passages.title: The search for the real thing
paragraphs: In the folk revival of the mid-twentieth century, young urban musicians traveled to rural communities in search of old songs and the people who still sang them. What they valued above all was authenticity: music that had passed from singer to singer, untouched by commerce or the recording studio. A singer who had learned a ballad from her grandmother was authentic; a singer who had learned it from a record was, at best, an imitation.

The irony is that the revival depended on the very technologies it distrusted. Collectors carried portable recorders; their recordings were pressed into records; and many of the revival's most admired performers learned their repertoire from those records. Even the rural singers were rarely as isolated as their admirers imagined. Many had heard the radio for decades and had absorbed popular songs alongside traditional ones, a mixture the collectors often quietly left off their tapes.

It would be easy to conclude that authenticity was simply a myth, a story urban audiences told themselves about rural people. But that conclusion is too quick. The revival's preoccupation with authenticity had real effects: it brought attention, income and sometimes a late-career audience to musicians who would otherwise have remained unknown, and it preserved songs that might otherwise have disappeared.

Perhaps the better lesson is that authenticity is less a property of a song than a relationship between a performer and a tradition. A singer who learns an old ballad from a record, studies its history and performs it with care may stand in a more genuine relation to the tradition than one who sings it by rote. What made the revival's best musicians admirable was not the purity of their sources but the seriousness of their attention.

passages.title: Speaking a language back to life
paragraphs: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, many linguists estimate that around half may cease to be spoken by the end of this century. Most will not disappear in a dramatic event. They will fade quietly, as parents raise their children in a language that seems more useful, the language of school, of government and of the job market, until the last fluent speakers grow old.

The loss is often described in terms borrowed from biology: languages are said to be "endangered" and to "die," and their disappearance is compared to the extinction of species. The comparison captures something real. Each language encodes ways of describing the world, from the classification of plants to the grammar of kinship, that exist nowhere else. When it goes silent, that knowledge may go with it.

But the biological metaphor can mislead. A species, once extinct, cannot return. A language can. Modern Hebrew, revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries after many centuries of use mainly in prayer and scholarship, is the most famous case, and smaller revivals are under way from Wales to New Zealand. Languages persist in recordings, texts and the memories of elders, and communities can choose to speak them again.

That choice, rather than the language itself, is the heart of the matter. Revitalization succeeds not when linguists document a grammar but when families decide to use the language at home and children hear it as the language of daily life. A language, unlike a species, lives in the decisions of the people who speak it, which is both why it can be lost so quietly and why it can be recovered.

passages.title: No free gifts
paragraphs: We like to think of a gift as the opposite of a trade. A trade is calculated; a gift is free. The anthropologist Marcel Mauss, in an influential essay published in 1925, argued that this contrast is largely an illusion. Surveying societies from the Pacific Northwest to Melanesia, he found that gifts everywhere created obligations: to give, to receive and, above all, to give back.

These obligations were not written down, but they were binding. A gift refused could be an insult; a gift unreturned could mean a loss of standing. In some societies, rival leaders competed to give away or even destroy great quantities of goods, gaining prestige by placing others in their debt. The gift, on Mauss's account, was a way of making and maintaining relationships, and relationships carry expectations.

It would be easy to read Mauss cynically, as if he had exposed generosity as a disguised form of self-interest. That reading misses his point. Mauss did not think the obligations of the gift made it insincere. He thought they made it social. A gift that created no bond, that left giver and receiver as strangers, would hardly be a gift at all.

Modern market societies have not abolished these obligations; they have confined them. We still keep track of dinner invitations owed and birthday presents exchanged, and we feel the sting when a favor is not returned. What has changed is that much of economic life now runs on transactions designed to leave no bond behind: a purchase that, once paid for, is finished. The gift persists in the spaces the market does not reach, and it reminds us of what those transactions leave out.

passages.title: Paper qualifications
paragraphs: Over the past half century, the educational requirements for many jobs have climbed. Positions that once required a high school diploma now ask for a college degree; jobs that once required a college degree now prefer a graduate one. The usual explanation is that work has grown more complex and demands more skill. For some occupations, that explanation is clearly right.

For others, it fits poorly. Studies of job postings have found employers demanding degrees for roles whose daily tasks have changed little, and some employers have dropped degree requirements for such roles without any visible decline in performance. If the work itself has not changed, something else must explain the rising bar.

One answer comes from the economics of signaling. A degree, on this view, matters less for what it teaches than for what it shows: that its holder could finish a long, demanding program. Employers who cannot easily judge an applicant's persistence or reliability use the degree as a stand-in. But a signal's value depends on its rarity. As more people earn degrees, a degree distinguishes less, and employers raise the requirement to sort applicants. Students then pursue more education to keep pace, and the cycle repeats.

The costs of this race fall unevenly. Additional years of schooling are easiest for those who can most readily afford them, so credential requirements can screen out capable applicants for reasons that have little to do with their capability. A requirement adopted as a convenient filter can thus become a barrier, one that tells employers less and less while asking applicants for more and more.

passages.title: The day of two noons
paragraphs: Before the late nineteenth century, time was local. Each town set its clocks by the sun, so that noon came when the sun stood highest overhead. Because the sun's position shifts as one travels east or west, noon in one city arrived a few minutes earlier or later than in the next. For most people, who rarely traveled far or fast, the differences hardly mattered.

The railroads changed that. A train crossing hundreds of miles passed through dozens of local times, and each railroad kept its own schedule, often based on the time at its headquarters. Travelers faced timetables listing several times for the same departure, and missed connections were common. On November 18, 1883, the railroads of the United States and Canada adopted a system of standard time zones, and clocks across the continent were reset. Some towns saw noon twice that day as their clocks were set back to the new standard.

The change was not imposed by government. It was a private agreement among railroad companies, and the federal government did not make the time zones law until 1918. Many towns adopted the new time immediately; some resisted for years, objecting that the railroads had no right to tell the sun when it was noon. Their protests reveal something easy to forget: the time on our clocks is a convention, chosen for coordination, not a fact read off the heavens.

Standard time is now so familiar that it seems natural, and that is precisely its success. Conventions work best when they become invisible. Yet the episode is a reminder that much of what organizes daily life was decided by particular people, for particular purposes, and could have been decided otherwise.

passages.title: Waiting in line
paragraphs: Few social arrangements are as ordinary, or as revealing, as the line. People who have never met agree, without discussion, to stand one behind another and to be served in the order they arrived. The principle of first come, first served is so widely accepted that cutting in line can provoke anger out of all proportion to the minutes lost.

The anger makes sense once we see what the line protects. A queue treats everyone in it as equal: the wealthy executive and the student stand in the same row and wait the same time. It is one of the few places in a market society where money does not, at least officially, buy priority. To cut in is not merely to take time from others; it is to declare oneself an exception to a rule that binds everyone else.

That equality has always had limits. Hospitals treat the sickest patients first, not the earliest arrivals, and few people object, because need is an accepted reason to depart from first come, first served. More troubling are departures based on money: express lanes sold at a premium, paid services that hold a place in line, and fees that let some travelers skip security queues. Each may be defended as efficient, since those who value their time most can pay to save it.

Yet efficiency is not the only value the line expresses. A society that auctions off places in every queue may serve its wealthier members faster, but it also teaches everyone that waiting is for those who cannot pay. Whether that lesson is worth the time it saves is not a technical question. It is a question about what kind of equality a society wants its everyday arrangements to express.

passages.title: Why we tip
paragraphs: Tipping is an odd custom when examined closely. A diner pays the listed price for a meal and then adds a sum that is nominally voluntary but socially required, calculated as a percentage of the bill rather than of the effort the server expended. Economists have long puzzled over why customers tip at all, particularly in restaurants they will never visit again, where no future service depends on their generosity.

The standard explanation is that tips function as a system of monitoring. Because a manager cannot watch every table, the restaurant delegates the evaluation of service to customers, who reward attentiveness and punish neglect. On this account, tipping persists because it is efficient: it aligns the server's incentives with the customer's satisfaction at almost no cost to the employer.

The evidence fits this account poorly. Studies of restaurant bills find that the size of a tip is only weakly related to customers' own ratings of the service they received. Tips vary far more with the size of the party, the weather, and the server's appearance and friendliness than with the speed or accuracy of the service. If tips are a monitoring system, they are a remarkably noisy one.

A better explanation may be that tipping is sustained less by calculation than by norms. Customers tip because they feel they ought to, and because failing to tip invites the disapproval of servers, companions and their own consciences. This view has an uncomfortable implication. If tips reflect customers' feelings and biases more than the quality of the work, then a system defended as rewarding merit may in practice distribute income according to factors that have little to do with merit at all.

passages.title: Eyes on the street
paragraphs: The planners who rebuilt many cities in the mid-twentieth century believed that safety came from order. Streets would be wide, buildings set back behind lawns, and homes separated from shops and offices so that each part of the city could do its job undisturbed. The result, in many neighborhoods, was streets that were tidy, quiet and, for long stretches of the day, empty.

Empty streets turned out to be dangerous streets. A sidewalk is safe, one influential critic argued, not because police patrol it but because people use it: shopkeepers standing in their doorways, residents glancing out of their windows, children playing, neighbors walking to the corner store. These "eyes on the street" belong to people who are not paid to watch and are not watching on purpose, yet together they create a kind of informal surveillance that deters crime and reassures strangers.

The idea has been enormously influential, but it is sometimes misunderstood. It does not claim that any crowd makes a street safe, or that density alone produces vigilance. The eyes in question belong to people with some stake in the street, who know which faces are familiar and who will intervene, or at least call for help, when something goes wrong. A busy highway interchange draws thousands of people a day, yet no one there is watching the street in this sense.

Nor does the idea imply that informal surveillance is always benign. The same neighbors who notice a stranger in trouble may also notice, and resent, a stranger who looks different from them. The vigilance that protects can also exclude. Those who would revive lively streets must therefore attend not only to how many eyes are on the street but to whose eyes they are and what they are looking for.

passages.title: Counting the people
paragraphs: A modern census asks every household a short list of questions and returns, years later, as tables: so many people of this age, so many in that occupation, so many in each district. The tables seem to describe the population as it simply is. But the categories that organize them were not discovered in nature; they were invented, argued over and revised, and each revision changed what the state could see.

Early censuses were often designed for narrow purposes, such as counting men who could be taxed or conscripted, and they recorded little else. As states took on new responsibilities for public health, education and welfare, they began to ask new questions about occupation, literacy, housing and disease. Each new category made a previously invisible group visible to administrators, and visibility had consequences. A government that could count the unemployed could design programs for them; it could also be blamed for their number.

Categories also shaped the people they described. When a census offered a fixed list of occupations or ethnic labels, respondents had to fit themselves into it, and over time some came to identify with the labels they had been given. Administrative convenience, in other words, could harden into social identity. Groups that had once been fluid or overlapping acquired sharp boundaries simply because the forms required a single answer.

None of this means that census figures are fictions. They are among the most valuable records a society keeps. But they are best read as the products of particular choices, made by particular people for particular ends. To read a census table well is to ask not only what it shows but what its makers wanted to know, and what they were content to leave unseen.

passages.title: The pot that goes around
paragraphs: In many parts of the world, groups of friends, coworkers or neighbors form what economists call rotating savings and credit associations. Each member contributes a fixed sum at regular meetings, and each time the whole pot goes to one member, until everyone has received it once. The arrangement is simple, and to an outside observer it can seem puzzling. Members who receive the pot late in the cycle would have done as well, or better, saving the money on their own or depositing it in a bank, where it would earn interest.

One explanation is that the associations serve people without access to banks. For those excluded from formal credit, receiving the pot early is like getting an interest-free loan, and even those who receive it late get something they could not easily produce alone: a lump sum large enough to buy a sewing machine, pay school fees or fix a roof. This is surely part of the story. But such associations flourish even among people who have bank accounts, and they persist in cities where banks are plentiful.

A second explanation looks to the difficulty of saving. Money kept at home is easily spent, on one's own wants or on the requests of relatives who know it is there. A commitment to the group turns saving from a private intention into a public obligation, enforced by the members' knowledge of one another and by the shame of failing to pay. The association's apparent inefficiency is, on this view, its point: members pay a small price in lost interest to buy a discipline they could not otherwise achieve.

Neither account captures what members themselves often emphasize, which is the meeting. The regular gathering is a place to exchange news, find work and reaffirm ties of trust. An association is therefore not only a financial device but also a social institution, and its value to members cannot be read off its interest rate.

passages.title: Inventing the weekend
paragraphs: The weekend seems like a natural feature of the calendar, but it is a recent and hard-won invention. In much of the industrializing world in the nineteenth century, factory workers labored six days a week, often for twelve hours a day or more, with Sunday reserved for church and rest. The idea that workers were entitled to a second free day would have struck many employers as absurd.

The free Saturday arrived in pieces. In some English industrial towns, workers had long taken an unofficial day off on Monday, known with grim humor as "Saint Monday," recovering from Sunday or simply refusing to return. Employers, frustrated by the absences, began to offer a deal: a half-day off on Saturday in exchange for reliable attendance on Monday. Meanwhile, labor unions campaigned for shorter hours, and religious groups, some of which observed a Saturday Sabbath, lent their support for their own reasons.

What finally made the full two-day weekend standard was less a single victory than a convergence of interests. Unions wanted leisure; some industrialists came to believe that rested workers were more productive; and a growing consumer economy needed people with free time in which to shop, travel and attend entertainments. By the middle of the twentieth century, the five-day week had become the norm in much of the industrialized world.

Seeing the weekend as an invention has a practical consequence. Arrangements that were negotiated can be renegotiated. As work spreads into evenings and weekends through phones and on-demand jobs, boundaries that once seemed fixed are blurring again. Whether the weekend survives may depend, as its creation did, on whether the interests of workers and employers can again be brought together.

passages.title: The translator's freedom
paragraphs: It is often said that a translation should be faithful to its original, as though fidelity were a single, obvious virtue. But a translator of poetry quickly discovers that fidelity pulls in several directions at once. A line may be faithful to the literal meaning of its source and false to its music; it may preserve the rhyme and lose the joke. Every translation is therefore a record of choices about which kinds of faithfulness matter most.

Some critics respond by demanding that translators stay as close as possible to the literal sense, on the grounds that the reader of a translation deserves to know what the poet actually said. This position has the appeal of modesty: the translator, on this view, is a servant who should not presume to improve on a master. Yet modesty can conceal its own presumption. To decide that literal sense is what the poet "actually said" is already to rank meaning above sound, rhythm and tone, a ranking many poets would reject.

The alternative is not license. A translator who rewrites freely, substituting her own images for the poet's, has produced a new poem, perhaps a fine one, but she has abandoned the reader who wanted access to the original. The most persuasive translations I know are neither literal nor free in this sense. They begin from a judgment about what is most alive in the original (its argument, its wit, its sorrow) and they spend their fidelity there, accepting losses elsewhere.

Readers can hold translators to account only if those judgments are made visible. A brief note explaining what the translator chose to preserve, and what she let go, would do more for the honest reader than any amount of insistence on fidelity in the abstract.

knowledgePoints.title: Strong acid and base pH
knowledgePoints.front: What is the pH of 0.001 M HCl? Of 0.001 M NaOH?
knowledgePoints.back: Strong acids dissociate fully, so pH = −log[H⁺] = 3. For strong bases, pOH = −log[OH⁻] = 3 and pH = 14 − 3 = 11 (at 25 °C).

knowledgePoints.title: Dilution
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find a concentration after dilution?
knowledgePoints.back: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where V₂ is the final total volume. Dilution always lowers concentration.

knowledgePoints.title: Molar volume at STP
knowledgePoints.front: What volume does one mole of ideal gas occupy at STP (0 °C, 1 atm)?
knowledgePoints.back: 22.4 L. Moles = volume ÷ 22.4 L/mol at STP.

knowledgePoints.title: Combined gas law
knowledgePoints.front: How does an ideal gas’s volume respond to pressure and temperature?
knowledgePoints.back: PV/T is constant, so V ∝ T/P: volume rises with kelvin temperature and falls with pressure.

knowledgePoints.title: Electric power
knowledgePoints.front: What power does a resistor dissipate?
knowledgePoints.back: P = IV = I²R = V²/R. At fixed resistance, doubling the voltage quadruples the power.

knowledgePoints.title: Capacitors
knowledgePoints.front: How much charge and energy does a charged capacitor store?
knowledgePoints.back: Q = CV and U = ½CV² (= ½QV).

knowledgePoints.title: Coulomb’s law
knowledgePoints.front: How does the electric force between two charges scale?
knowledgePoints.back: F = kq₁q₂/r²: proportional to each charge, inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

knowledgePoints.title: Horizontal launches
knowledgePoints.front: A ball rolls off a ledge horizontally. What sets its flight time?
knowledgePoints.back: Only the height: t = √(2h/g). Horizontal distance = horizontal speed × t.

knowledgePoints.title: Kinetic energy
knowledgePoints.front: How does kinetic energy scale with speed and mass, and how fast is an object after falling h?
knowledgePoints.back: KE = ½mv², so it scales with v². Energy conservation gives v = √(2gh), independent of mass.

knowledgePoints.title: Work and power
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find the average power of a force?
knowledgePoints.back: Work W = Fd (force along the motion; lifting: mgh). Power P = W/t.

knowledgePoints.title: Pressure at depth
knowledgePoints.front: What is the pressure at a depth h in a fluid?
knowledgePoints.back: Gauge pressure = ρgh. Absolute pressure adds the surface pressure (about 1 atm ≈ 100 kPa).

knowledgePoints.title: Floating objects
knowledgePoints.front: What fraction of a floating object is submerged?
knowledgePoints.back: Its density divided by the fluid’s density (ρ_object/ρ_fluid).

knowledgePoints.title: Magnification
knowledgePoints.front: How do you read magnification for a lens or mirror?
knowledgePoints.back: m = −dᵢ/dₒ. Negative means inverted, |m| < 1 means smaller than the object.

knowledgePoints.title: Lens power
knowledgePoints.front: What is a lens’s power in diopters?
knowledgePoints.back: P = 1/f with f in meters. Converging lenses are positive, diverging lenses negative.

knowledgePoints.title: Sound level
knowledgePoints.front: How do decibels relate to intensity?
knowledgePoints.back: β = 10 log(I/I₀): every 10× in intensity adds 10 dB.

knowledgePoints.title: Half-life
knowledgePoints.front: How much of a radioactive sample remains after n half-lives?
knowledgePoints.back: (½)ⁿ of the original. Three half-lives leave one-eighth.

knowledgePoints.title: Standard cell potential
knowledgePoints.front: How do you get E°cell from standard reduction potentials?
knowledgePoints.back: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), both as reduction potentials. Never multiply by stoichiometric coefficients.

knowledgePoints.title: Rate laws
knowledgePoints.front: Rate = k[A]²[B]. What happens if [A] doubles?
knowledgePoints.back: The rate changes by 2² = 4×. Each concentration factor is raised to its order.

knowledgePoints.title: Moles from mass
knowledgePoints.front: How do you convert grams to moles?
knowledgePoints.back: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass (g/mol).

knowledgePoints.title: Periods of oscillation
knowledgePoints.front: How do a pendulum’s and a spring’s periods depend on their properties?
knowledgePoints.back: Pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass. Spring: T = 2π√(m/k).

knowledgePoints.title: Mendelian ratios
knowledgePoints.front: Aa × Aa: what fraction of offspring are aa? What fraction of the dominant-looking offspring are carriers?
knowledgePoints.back: ¼ are aa. Among dominant-phenotype offspring (AA, Aa, Aa), ⅔ are carriers.

knowledgePoints.title: X-linked inheritance
knowledgePoints.front: A carrier mother and an unaffected father have a son. What’s the chance he’s affected by an X-linked recessive trait?
knowledgePoints.back: ½. Sons get their only X from their mother; daughters of an unaffected father aren’t affected.

knowledgePoints.title: Michaelis–Menten
knowledgePoints.front: What is V₀ when [S] = Km? When [S] = 3Km?
knowledgePoints.back: V₀ = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]): ½Vmax at [S] = Km, ¾Vmax at 3Km, 9/10 Vmax at 9Km.

knowledgePoints.title: Lineweaver–Burk plots
knowledgePoints.front: What do the intercepts of a Lineweaver–Burk plot give?
knowledgePoints.back: y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax.

knowledgePoints.title: Isoelectric point
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find an amino acid’s pI?
knowledgePoints.back: Average the two pKa values on either side of the neutral form: the two lowest for acidic side chains, the two highest for basic ones.

knowledgePoints.title: Nernst equation
knowledgePoints.front: How do you estimate an ion’s equilibrium potential at body temperature?
knowledgePoints.back: E = (61.5 mV / z) × log([out]/[in]). K⁺ is about −90 mV; Na⁺ about +60 mV.

knowledgePoints.title: Cardiac output
knowledgePoints.front: How are cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction calculated?
knowledgePoints.back: SV = EDV − ESV; CO = HR × SV; EF = SV/EDV.

knowledgePoints.title: Ventilation
knowledgePoints.front: What’s the difference between minute and alveolar ventilation?
knowledgePoints.back: Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate. Alveolar ventilation subtracts dead space: (VT − VD) × rate.

knowledgePoints.title: Chargaff’s rules
knowledgePoints.front: In double-stranded DNA that is 20% adenine, what fraction is guanine?
knowledgePoints.back: A = T and G = C, so A + T = 40% and G = C = 30% each.

knowledgePoints.title: The 68–95–99.7 rule
knowledgePoints.front: In a normal distribution, what share of scores falls within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean?
knowledgePoints.back: About 68%, 95% and 99.7%. So about 16% lie above +1 SD and 2.5% above +2 SD.

knowledgePoints.title: z-scores
knowledgePoints.front: How do you convert a raw score to a z-score?
knowledgePoints.back: z = (score − mean)/SD. A z of +2 sits near the 97.5th percentile.

knowledgePoints.title: Mean, median and skew
knowledgePoints.front: In a right-skewed distribution, how do the mean and median compare?
knowledgePoints.back: The long right tail pulls the mean above the median (and the median above the mode). The median resists outliers.

knowledgePoints.title: Reading correlations
knowledgePoints.front: Which is the stronger correlation: r = −0.8 or r = +0.5? How much variance does r = 0.5 explain?
knowledgePoints.back: Strength is |r|, so −0.8 is stronger. r² is the variance explained: 0.5² = 25%.

knowledgePoints.title: Probability of independent events
knowledgePoints.front: How do you combine probabilities of independent events?
knowledgePoints.back: Both happen: multiply. At least one happens: 1 − P(neither).

knowledgePoints.title: Weber’s law
knowledgePoints.front: If the just-noticeable difference for 100 g is 2 g, what is it for 400 g?
knowledgePoints.back: 8 g. The JND is a constant fraction (here 2%) of the original stimulus.

knowledgePoints.title: Demographic rates
knowledgePoints.front: How are crude birth rates and doubling times calculated?
knowledgePoints.back: Crude rate = events per 1,000 people per year. Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ annual growth rate (%).

knowledgePoints.title: Oxidizing and reducing agents
knowledgePoints.front: PCC vs. chromic acid; NaBH₄ vs. LiAlH₄?
knowledgePoints.back: PCC stops a primary alcohol at the aldehyde; chromic acid goes on to the carboxylic acid. NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones only; LiAlH₄ also reduces esters and acids.

knowledgePoints.title: IR spectroscopy landmarks
knowledgePoints.front: Where do C=O, alcohol O–H and carboxylic acid O–H absorb?
knowledgePoints.back: C=O: sharp, strong, about 1700 cm⁻¹. Alcohol O–H: broad, 3200–3600. Carboxylic acid O–H: very broad, 2500–3300. Nitrile C≡N: about 2250.

knowledgePoints.title: ¹H NMR chemical shifts
knowledgePoints.front: Where do aldehyde, carboxylic acid and aromatic protons appear?
knowledgePoints.back: Carboxylic acid O–H: 10–12 ppm. Aldehyde C–H: 9–10. Aromatic: 6.5–8. H on carbon bonded to O: 3.3–4. Plain alkyl: 0.9–1.5.

knowledgePoints.title: Separation techniques
knowledgePoints.front: Which chromatography separates by size, which by charge, and which by specific binding?
knowledgePoints.back: Gel filtration: size (large elute first). Ion exchange: charge. Affinity: specific binding to an immobilized ligand. SDS-PAGE: mass of denatured proteins.

knowledgePoints.title: Derived SI units
knowledgePoints.front: Write the newton, joule, watt and pascal in base units.
knowledgePoints.back: N = kg·m/s². J = N·m = kg·m²/s². W = J/s = kg·m²/s³. Pa = N/m² = kg/(m·s²).

knowledgePoints.title: Electrical units
knowledgePoints.front: Express the volt, ohm, farad and ampere in terms of other units.
knowledgePoints.back: V = J/C. Ω = V/A. F = C/V. A = C/s. The tesla is N/(A·m).

knowledgePoints.title: Types of radioactive decay
knowledgePoints.front: How does each decay type change the atomic number (Z) and mass number (A)?
knowledgePoints.back: Alpha: A −4, Z −2. Beta-minus: Z +1. Positron emission and electron capture: Z −1. Gamma: no change.

knowledgePoints.title: Kinds of isomers
knowledgePoints.front: Enantiomers vs. diastereomers?
knowledgePoints.back: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images (opposite configuration at every stereocenter). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that aren’t mirror images.

knowledgePoints.title: Bonds that build biomolecules
knowledgePoints.front: Which bond links each kind of monomer?
knowledgePoints.back: Sugars: glycosidic. Amino acids: peptide. Nucleotides: phosphodiester. Fatty acids to glycerol: ester.

knowledgePoints.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
knowledgePoints.front: Order the EM spectrum from lowest to highest frequency.
knowledgePoints.back: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Energy rises with frequency (E = hf).

knowledgePoints.title: Intermolecular forces
knowledgePoints.front: Rank the intermolecular forces from weakest to strongest.
knowledgePoints.back: London dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding < ion–dipole. Dispersion grows with molecular size and can dominate in big molecules.

knowledgePoints.title: Hybridization
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find an atom’s hybridization?
knowledgePoints.back: Count electron domains (bonds count once, lone pairs count once): 2 = sp, 3 = sp², 4 = sp³, 5 = sp³d.

knowledgePoints.title: VSEPR shapes
knowledgePoints.front: Why is water bent but CO₂ linear?
knowledgePoints.back: Water’s O has two bonds and two lone pairs (four domains, bent). CO₂’s C has two double bonds and no lone pairs (two domains, linear).

knowledgePoints.title: Acid–base definitions
knowledgePoints.front: Brønsted–Lowry vs. Lewis acids?
knowledgePoints.back: Brønsted–Lowry acids donate protons. Lewis acids accept electron pairs; Lewis bases donate them. Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base.

knowledgePoints.title: The gas laws
knowledgePoints.front: Which variables does each gas law hold constant?
knowledgePoints.back: Boyle: P ∝ 1/V (constant n, T). Charles: V ∝ T (constant n, P). Gay-Lussac: P ∝ T (constant n, V). Avogadro: V ∝ n (constant P, T).

knowledgePoints.title: Thermodynamic processes
knowledgePoints.front: In which process does a gas do no work, and in which is ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas?
knowledgePoints.back: Isochoric (constant volume): no work, so ΔU = Q. Isothermal (ideal gas): ΔU = 0, so Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W.

knowledgePoints.title: Mirrors and lenses
knowledgePoints.front: Which optical elements can only form upright, reduced, virtual images?
knowledgePoints.back: Convex mirrors and diverging lenses. Concave mirrors and converging lenses can form real or virtual images depending on where the object sits.

knowledgePoints.title: Wave phenomena
knowledgePoints.front: What causes beats, and what is their frequency?
knowledgePoints.back: Two waves of slightly different frequency interfere, alternating between constructive and destructive. The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies.

knowledgePoints.title: Families of the periodic table
knowledgePoints.front: What makes alkali metals so reactive and noble gases so inert?
knowledgePoints.back: Alkali metals have one valence electron to lose (low ionization energy). Noble gases have full valence shells and the highest ionization energies in each period.

knowledgePoints.title: Where hormones come from
knowledgePoints.front: Which hormones does the posterior pituitary release, and where are they made?
knowledgePoints.back: ADH and oxytocin. They are made in the hypothalamus and carried down axons to the posterior pituitary, which releases them into the blood.

knowledgePoints.title: What hormones do
knowledgePoints.front: PTH vs. calcitonin; oxytocin vs. prolactin?
knowledgePoints.back: PTH raises blood Ca²⁺; calcitonin lowers it. Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it (and drives labor contractions).

knowledgePoints.title: Steroid, peptide and amine hormones
knowledgePoints.front: How do steroid and peptide hormones differ in receptor, transport and speed?
knowledgePoints.back: Steroids: lipid-soluble, carried by proteins, intracellular receptors, slow gene effects. Peptides: water-soluble, travel free, surface receptors and second messengers, fast.

knowledgePoints.title: Amino acid essentials
knowledgePoints.front: Which amino acids are acidic, which are basic, and which one is achiral?
knowledgePoints.back: Acidic: Asp (D), Glu (E). Basic: Lys (K), Arg (R), His (H). Glycine is achiral. Cys forms disulfides; Pro breaks helices.

knowledgePoints.title: Organelles and their jobs
knowledgePoints.front: Rough ER vs. smooth ER?
knowledgePoints.back: Rough ER: ribosomes making secreted and membrane proteins. Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification and Ca²⁺ storage.

knowledgePoints.title: Regulated enzymes of metabolism
knowledgePoints.front: Name the rate-limiting enzymes of glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and cholesterol synthesis.
knowledgePoints.back: Glycolysis: PFK-1. Citric acid cycle: isocitrate dehydrogenase. Cholesterol: HMG-CoA reductase (the statin target). Pentose phosphate pathway: G6PD.

knowledgePoints.title: Digestive enzymes
knowledgePoints.front: How is trypsinogen activated, and why does that matter?
knowledgePoints.back: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic zymogens.

knowledgePoints.title: Immune cell roles
knowledgePoints.front: Which cells kill infected cells, and which kill cells that hide their MHC I?
knowledgePoints.back: Cytotoxic (CD8⁺) T cells kill cells showing foreign peptide on MHC I. Natural killer cells kill cells that have lost MHC I.

knowledgePoints.title: Nephron segments
knowledgePoints.front: Which nephron segment is permeable to water but not salt, and which is the reverse?
knowledgePoints.back: Descending limb: water out, salt stays. Thick ascending limb: salt pumped out, water can’t follow. Together they build the medullary gradient.

knowledgePoints.title: Germ layer derivatives
knowledgePoints.front: Which germ layer forms the adrenal medulla, and which forms the adrenal cortex?
knowledgePoints.back: Medulla: ectoderm (neural crest). Cortex: mesoderm. Endoderm lines the gut and lungs and forms the liver and pancreas.

knowledgePoints.title: Neurotransmitters
knowledgePoints.front: Which neurotransmitter is the brain’s main excitatory signal, and which is its main inhibitory one?
knowledgePoints.back: Glutamate excites; GABA inhibits. Acetylcholine runs the neuromuscular junction; dopamine handles reward and movement.

knowledgePoints.title: The path of blood through the heart
knowledgePoints.front: Trace blood from the venae cavae to the aorta.
knowledgePoints.back: Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral → left ventricle → aorta.

knowledgePoints.title: Inheritance patterns
knowledgePoints.front: Incomplete dominance vs. codominance?
knowledgePoints.back: Incomplete dominance blends (red × white → pink). Codominance shows both fully (type AB blood).

knowledgePoints.title: Mechanisms of evolution
knowledgePoints.front: Founder effect vs. bottleneck effect?
knowledgePoints.back: Both are genetic drift. Founder: a few individuals start a new population. Bottleneck: a disaster shrinks an existing one. Either way, allele frequencies shift by chance.

knowledgePoints.title: Receptor types
knowledgePoints.front: Which receptor type acts in milliseconds, and which changes gene expression?
knowledgePoints.back: Ligand-gated ion channels act in milliseconds. GPCRs and RTKs use signaling cascades (seconds to minutes). Intracellular receptors change transcription (hours).

knowledgePoints.title: Membrane transport
knowledgePoints.front: Primary vs. secondary active transport?
knowledgePoints.back: Primary uses ATP directly (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase). Secondary uses an ion gradient made by a primary pump to move another solute uphill (SGLT, Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger).

knowledgePoints.title: Bone cells
knowledgePoints.front: Osteoblasts vs. osteoclasts?
knowledgePoints.back: Osteoblasts build bone matrix. Osteoclasts resorb bone and release Ca²⁺. PTH activates osteoclasts indirectly; calcitonin inhibits them.

knowledgePoints.title: Sarcomere proteins
knowledgePoints.front: How does Ca²⁺ switch on contraction?
knowledgePoints.back: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin off actin’s myosin-binding sites. ATP binding then releases each myosin head so the cycle can repeat.

knowledgePoints.title: Bacterial gene transfer
knowledgePoints.front: Transformation vs. transduction vs. conjugation?
knowledgePoints.back: Transformation: naked DNA taken up. Transduction: DNA carried by a phage. Conjugation: DNA passed through a pilus from cell to cell.

knowledgePoints.title: Cell cycle and mitosis
knowledgePoints.front: What happens in each phase of mitosis?
knowledgePoints.back: Prophase: chromosomes condense, envelope breaks down. Metaphase: chromosomes line up. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate. Telophase: envelopes re-form.

knowledgePoints.title: Meiosis I vs. meiosis II
knowledgePoints.front: In which division do homologs separate, and in which do sister chromatids separate?
knowledgePoints.back: Homologs separate in anaphase I (the reductional division). Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II, as in mitosis.

knowledgePoints.title: Early embryonic stages
knowledgePoints.front: Order the early stages of development.
knowledgePoints.back: Zygote → morula (solid ball) → blastocyst (implants; inner cell mass + trophoblast) → gastrula (germ layers) → neurula (neural tube).

knowledgePoints.title: Hormones of the menstrual cycle
knowledgePoints.front: What does each hormone do across the menstrual cycle?
knowledgePoints.back: FSH grows follicles; follicles make estrogen; an LH surge triggers ovulation; the corpus luteum makes progesterone; hCG from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum alive.

knowledgePoints.title: Carbohydrates and lipids
knowledgePoints.front: Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
knowledgePoints.back: Starch has α-1,4 (and α-1,6) glycosidic bonds that amylase cuts. Cellulose has β-1,4 bonds, and humans lack an enzyme to break them.

knowledgePoints.title: Vitamins
knowledgePoints.front: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
knowledgePoints.back: A, D, E and K. They are stored in fat and the liver, so they can build up to toxic levels.

knowledgePoints.title: Group processes
knowledgePoints.front: Social facilitation vs. social loafing vs. deindividuation: what does each need?
knowledgePoints.back: Facilitation: an audience boosts well-learned tasks. Loafing: pooled, untracked effort drops. Deindividuation: anonymity in a crowd lowers restraint.

knowledgePoints.title: Attribution biases
knowledgePoints.front: Fundamental attribution error vs. actor–observer bias vs. self-serving bias?
knowledgePoints.back: FAE: others’ behavior → their character. Actor–observer: my behavior → situation, yours → character. Self-serving: my wins → me, my losses → situation.

knowledgePoints.title: Persuasion and attitude change
knowledgePoints.front: Foot-in-the-door vs. door-in-the-face, and the two routes to persuasion?
knowledgePoints.back: FITD: small request first. DITF: big refused request first. Central route: argument quality, lasting change. Peripheral route: surface cues, fleeting change.

knowledgePoints.title: Defense mechanisms
knowledgePoints.front: Repression vs. suppression; projection vs. displacement vs. sublimation?
knowledgePoints.back: Repression is unconscious, suppression deliberate. Projection moves a feeling onto another person; displacement moves it to a safer target; sublimation channels it into something valued.

knowledgePoints.title: Reinforcement and punishment
knowledgePoints.front: Positive/negative reinforcement vs. punishment: how do you tell them apart?
knowledgePoints.back: Reinforcement raises a behavior, punishment lowers it. Positive adds a stimulus, negative removes one. Negative reinforcement is not punishment.

knowledgePoints.title: Reinforcement schedules
knowledgePoints.front: Which schedule gives the highest response rate and the most resistance to extinction?
knowledgePoints.back: Variable ratio (slot machines). Fixed ratio: pause after each reward. Fixed interval: scalloped responding. Variable interval: slow and steady.

knowledgePoints.title: Elements of classical conditioning
knowledgePoints.front: Which stimulus is “conditioned”: the one that triggered the response from the start, or the one that learned to?
knowledgePoints.back: The one that learned to. The UCS (food, pain) triggers the UCR naturally; a neutral stimulus paired with it becomes the CS, which triggers the CR.

knowledgePoints.title: Generalization, discrimination, extinction
knowledgePoints.front: What is spontaneous recovery, and what does it show about extinction?
knowledgePoints.back: After extinction and a rest, the CR briefly returns. Extinction suppresses the learned response; it doesn’t erase it.

knowledgePoints.title: Memory phenomena
knowledgePoints.front: Proactive vs. retroactive interference; context- vs. state-dependent memory?
knowledgePoints.back: Proactive: old learning blocks new. Retroactive: new learning blocks old. Context-dependent: same place helps recall. State-dependent: same internal state helps recall.

knowledgePoints.title: Threats to validity
knowledgePoints.front: Hawthorne effect vs. demand characteristics vs. placebo effect?
knowledgePoints.back: Hawthorne: behavior changes because people know they’re observed. Demand characteristics: participants guess the hypothesis and act to fit it. Placebo: expecting treatment brings improvement.

knowledgePoints.title: Study designs
knowledgePoints.front: Cohort vs. case–control: which direction does each look?
knowledgePoints.back: Cohort: start from exposure, follow forward to outcomes. Case–control: start from the outcome, look back for exposures (good for rare diseases).

knowledgePoints.title: Erikson’s psychosocial stages
knowledgePoints.front: List Erikson’s eight stages in order.
knowledgePoints.back: Trust vs. mistrust, autonomy vs. shame, initiative vs. guilt, industry vs. inferiority, identity vs. role confusion, intimacy vs. isolation, generativity vs. stagnation, integrity vs. despair.

knowledgePoints.title: Brain regions and functions
knowledgePoints.front: Broca’s vs. Wernicke’s aphasia: which area does what?
knowledgePoints.back: Broca’s area (frontal lobe) produces speech: damage gives slow, effortful speech with intact comprehension. Wernicke’s area (temporal lobe) comprehends: damage gives fluent nonsense.

knowledgePoints.title: Sleep stages
knowledgePoints.front: Which EEG waves go with wakefulness, N1, N2, N3 and REM?
knowledgePoints.back: Awake alert: beta. Relaxed: alpha. N1: theta. N2: sleep spindles and K-complexes. N3: delta. REM: beta-like, with muscle atonia and dreaming.

knowledgePoints.title: Thresholds, adaptation and processing
knowledgePoints.front: Top-down vs. bottom-up processing?
knowledgePoints.back: Bottom-up builds a percept from raw features. Top-down uses expectations and context to interpret input.

knowledgePoints.title: Signal detection theory
knowledgePoints.front: Name the four outcomes of signal detection theory.
knowledgePoints.back: Signal present: hit (“yes”) or miss (“no”). Signal absent: false alarm (“yes”) or correct rejection (“no”).

knowledgePoints.title: Sociological theories
knowledgePoints.front: Functionalism vs. conflict theory vs. symbolic interactionism?
knowledgePoints.back: Functionalism: parts keep society stable. Conflict theory: groups compete for power and resources. Symbolic interactionism: meaning is built in everyday interaction.

knowledgePoints.title: Mobility and capital
knowledgePoints.front: Intergenerational vs. intragenerational mobility; cultural vs. social capital?
knowledgePoints.back: Intergenerational: between parents and children. Intragenerational: within one lifetime. Cultural capital: knowledge, tastes and credentials. Social capital: useful relationships.

knowledgePoints.title: Roles and statuses
knowledgePoints.front: Role conflict vs. role strain?
knowledgePoints.back: Role conflict: two different roles clash. Role strain: one role makes competing demands.

knowledgePoints.title: Theories of emotion
knowledgePoints.front: James–Lange vs. Cannon–Bard vs. Schachter–Singer?
knowledgePoints.back: James–Lange: arousal, then emotion. Cannon–Bard: arousal and emotion together. Schachter–Singer: arousal plus a cognitive label creates the emotion.

knowledgePoints.title: Theories of motivation
knowledgePoints.front: Why can’t drive-reduction theory explain skydiving?
knowledgePoints.back: Skydiving raises arousal instead of reducing a need. Arousal theory explains it: people seek an optimal level of arousal.

knowledgePoints.title: Recognizing psychological disorders
knowledgePoints.front: GAD vs. panic disorder vs. specific phobia?
knowledgePoints.back: GAD: constant, wide-ranging worry for 6+ months. Panic disorder: unexpected panic attacks plus fear of more. Specific phobia: intense fear of one object or situation.

knowledgePoints.title: Buffer pH
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find a buffer's pH from its pKa and the base-to-acid ratio?
knowledgePoints.back: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Each tenfold increase in [A⁻]/[HA] raises the pH by 1 unit above the pKa.

knowledgePoints.title: Resistors in parallel
knowledgePoints.front: What's the equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel?
knowledgePoints.back: R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂), which is smaller than either resistor. Each branch has the full voltage, and the branch currents add.

knowledgePoints.title: Spontaneity and temperature
knowledgePoints.front: When is a reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0 spontaneous?
knowledgePoints.back: Above T = ΔH/ΔS, from ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Convert kJ to J (or J to kJ) first.

knowledgePoints.title: Continuity equation
knowledgePoints.front: A pipe narrows. What happens to the speed of the fluid?
knowledgePoints.back: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so speed rises in proportion to the drop in area. By Bernoulli's principle, pressure falls where speed rises.

knowledgePoints.title: Gas laws use kelvin
knowledgePoints.front: A rigid container of gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. What happens to the pressure?
knowledgePoints.back: Convert to kelvin: 300 K → 600 K. At constant volume P ∝ T, so pressure doubles.

knowledgePoints.title: Competitive inhibition
knowledgePoints.front: What does a competitive inhibitor do to Km and Vmax?
knowledgePoints.back: Km rises and Vmax is unchanged, because enough substrate can outcompete the inhibitor. Apparent Km = Km(1 + [I]/Ki).

knowledgePoints.title: Telling inhibitors apart
knowledgePoints.front: How do noncompetitive and uncompetitive inhibition change Km and Vmax?
knowledgePoints.back: Noncompetitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged. Uncompetitive: Vmax and Km both fall. Competitive: Km rises, Vmax unchanged.

knowledgePoints.title: Reading Km from data
knowledgePoints.front: How do you read Km from a table of reaction rates?
knowledgePoints.back: Estimate Vmax from the plateau at high [S], then find the [S] where V₀ is half of Vmax.

knowledgePoints.title: Charged side chains
knowledgePoints.front: Which amino acid side chains are charged at pH 7.4?
knowledgePoints.back: Positive: lysine and arginine (histidine only partly). Negative: aspartate and glutamate.

knowledgePoints.title: Okazaki fragments
knowledgePoints.front: Why is the lagging strand made in fragments?
knowledgePoints.back: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so synthesis runs 5′→3′. On the lagging template that direction points away from the fork, so it's made in short Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer.

knowledgePoints.title: ADH and water balance
knowledgePoints.front: Which hormone conserves water when someone is dehydrated, and where is it released?
knowledgePoints.back: ADH (vasopressin). It's made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary, and inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct.

knowledgePoints.title: Hardy–Weinberg
knowledgePoints.front: The recessive phenotype frequency is q². How do you find the carrier frequency?
knowledgePoints.back: q = √(q²), p = 1 − q, and heterozygotes = 2pq.

knowledgePoints.title: Reinforcement and punishment
knowledgePoints.front: Removing something unpleasant to make a behavior more frequent is called…?
knowledgePoints.back: Negative reinforcement. Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it. "Positive" adds a stimulus; "negative" removes one.

knowledgePoints.title: Attribution biases
knowledgePoints.front: "When they're late, it's their character. When I'm late, it's the traffic." Which bias is this?
knowledgePoints.back: Actor–observer bias. The fundamental attribution error is only the half about judging other people.

knowledgePoints.title: Correlation vs. causation
knowledgePoints.front: A survey finds a correlation between two variables. What can it conclude?
knowledgePoints.back: An association only. Without an experiment, or controls for confounders, it can't show which variable (if either) causes the other.

knowledgePoints.title: Sociological perspectives
knowledgePoints.front: "Institutions persist because they keep society running smoothly." Which perspective is that?
knowledgePoints.back: Functionalism. Conflict theory stresses inequality and power; symbolic interactionism stresses everyday meanings and interactions.

knowledgePoints.title: CARS main idea
knowledgePoints.front: How do you test a CARS main-idea answer?
knowledgePoints.back: It must capture the author's overall claim, not a view the author argues against and not one paragraph's detail.

knowledgePoints.title: Why authors describe opposing views
knowledgePoints.front: Why would an author point out the appeal of a view the author rejects?
knowledgePoints.back: To concede its attraction before arguing against it. Look for the "Yet" or "But" that follows.

knowledgePoints.title: Applying the author's view
knowledgePoints.front: "Which practice would the author most likely endorse?" What are you matching?
knowledgePoints.back: The author's own recommendations and values, often in the last paragraph, not the views of critics the author rejects.

knowledgePoints.title: Challenging a claim
knowledgePoints.front: What does the right answer to "Which finding would most challenge the author's claim?" do?
knowledgePoints.back: It directly undercuts the claim's key support. Answers that are merely unrelated or mildly negative don't count.

knowledgePoints.title: Galvanic cells
knowledgePoints.front: In a galvanic cell, where does oxidation happen and which way do electrons flow?
knowledgePoints.back: "An Ox, Red Cat": oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Electrons flow from anode to cathode through the external wire.

knowledgePoints.title: Le Chatelier's principle
knowledgePoints.front: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), what shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?
knowledgePoints.back: Higher pressure (fewer gas moles on the product side), lower temperature, or adding a reactant. A catalyst speeds both directions and doesn't shift it.

knowledgePoints.title: Thin lens equation
knowledgePoints.front: How do you find where a converging lens forms an image?
knowledgePoints.back: 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ. A positive dᵢ is a real, inverted image on the far side of the lens.

knowledgePoints.title: Free fall
knowledgePoints.front: How long does an object dropped from rest take to fall a height h?
knowledgePoints.back: h = ½gt², so t = √(2h/g). The time doesn't depend on mass (ignoring air resistance).

knowledgePoints.title: Glycolysis regulation
knowledgePoints.front: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
knowledgePoints.back: Phosphofructokinase-1 (fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate). It's inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

knowledgePoints.title: Action potential phases
knowledgePoints.front: What drives depolarization and repolarization in an action potential?
knowledgePoints.back: Depolarization: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in. Repolarization: Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels let K⁺ out.

knowledgePoints.title: MHC and T cells
knowledgePoints.front: Which T cells kill infected cells, and which MHC do they read?
knowledgePoints.back: Cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells recognize antigen on MHC class I and kill the cell. Helper CD4⁺ T cells recognize MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells.

knowledgePoints.title: Context-dependent memory
knowledgePoints.front: Why do people recall more when tested in the room where they studied?
knowledgePoints.back: Encoding specificity: retrieval works best when cues at recall match those at encoding. External setting = context-dependent; internal state = state-dependent.

knowledgePoints.title: Piaget's stages
knowledgePoints.front: Which Piagetian milestone is missing when a child thinks a taller glass holds more juice?
knowledgePoints.back: Conservation, acquired in the concrete operational stage (about 7–11). Object permanence comes earlier (sensorimotor); abstract reasoning later (formal operational).

knowledgePoints.title: Cognitive dissonance
knowledgePoints.front: Why do people talk themselves into liking things they paid a lot for?
knowledgePoints.back: Cognitive dissonance: holding conflicting beliefs and actions is uncomfortable, so people change a belief to justify what they did (effort justification).

knowledgePoints.title: Supported inferences
knowledgePoints.front: What makes an answer a supported inference in CARS rather than a reasonable guess?
knowledgePoints.back: It must follow from specific words in the passage with little or no extra assumption. Find the line that supports it; if you can't, it's a guess.

knowledgePoints.title: The author's attitude
knowledgePoints.front: How do you pin down an author's attitude toward a view?
knowledgePoints.back: Look for evaluative words (praise, concession, irony, hedges like "perhaps") and for what the author ultimately endorses. Extreme answers (contempt, uncritical admiration) are usually wrong; mixed attitudes are common.
